lessons.title: What CRYPTO NOVA is and how it can help
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to explain in your own words what CRYPTO NOVA does — and what it doesn't promise.

cards.title: A helper that never sleeps
cards.text: CRYPTO NOVA is a computer system powered by artificial intelligence (AI). It watches the crypto market around the clock. Crypto, short for cryptocurrency, is digital money — bitcoin, for example. The system looks for good moments to trade, following its own rules. You can see every trade it makes in the app.
cards.example: In real life: a night guard watches a warehouse all night, but in the morning he needs to sleep. A program doesn't: it watches the market day and night.

cards.title: Rules tested on the past
cards.text: Before the system starts using a rule, it tests it on past prices. In other words, it checks what would have happened if the rule had been in use before. Every night it tries out new ideas and keeps only the ones that pass. But the past doesn't promise the future.
cards.example: In real life: a cook tries a new pie on the family first, and only then bakes it for guests. But even a tried-and-tested recipe sometimes flops.

cards.title: What's in the app
cards.text: At the bottom of the screen are the tabs: “Home”, “Futures”, “Spot” and “Learn”. In the middle is the NOVA AI icon, the assistant for your questions. Home has 6 more buttons, including “Piggy bank” and “Tour”. Tap the round profile icon at the top to open “Account”.
cards.example: In real life: it's like a shopping mall with several floors. You don't have to see everything at once. Start with one shop — the rest will wait.

cards.title: Start with the demo
cards.text: To begin, there's the demo: a practice portfolio with virtual money. The prices are real, but the money isn't. You can look around, try things and make mistakes with no risk. Real money only comes in when you connect your own exchange account yourself.
cards.example: In real life: at driving school, you start on a simulator. The wheel and the road feel real, but a mistake costs nothing.

cards.title: Honest about risk
cards.text: Crypto is risky: prices swing hard. The system can be wrong, and it does have losing trades. Good results in the past don't promise the same in the future. CRYPTO NOVA teaches and shows, but it doesn't give financial advice. The decision is always yours.
cards.example: In real life: the forecast says sunshine, but you take an umbrella anyway. A forecast helps, but it doesn't control the weather.

lessons.title: Two paths: calm and active
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand how the calm path differs from the active one, and you'll decide where to start.

cards.title: Two paths in one app
cards.text: There are two ways to use CRYPTO NOVA. The calm path: save a little at a time and hold major coins for years. That's the “Piggy bank” and “Spot”. The active path: follow fast trades that bet on prices rising or falling. That's “Futures”. You can pick one path or combine both.
cards.example: In real life: you can get to the countryside by train — slow but relaxed. Or by motorbike — faster, but more dangerous.

cards.title: The calm path: the Piggy bank
cards.text: The Piggy bank means buying a little bitcoin on a schedule. For example, $10 every week. You don't need to follow the news or guess the best day. This path suits people saving for retirement, their kids' education or a dream, who are happy to wait for years.
cards.example: In real life: parents put aside a little each month for their child's education. It's not much at a time, but after 10 years it adds up to a real sum.

cards.title: The active path: futures
cards.text: On the “Futures” tab, the system opens trades that bet on the price going up or down. Each one has an entry, a stop and a target. The stop is the price where the trade closes with a small loss. The target is the price where you take your profit. The risk here is higher: it takes knowledge and attention.
cards.example: In real life: fishing takes patience and skill. The fish don't always bite, and sometimes you go home empty-handed.

cards.title: Repeat or copy: you decide
cards.text: The system runs its own trades and shows them to you. You can repeat a trade in your own exchange account yourself, or turn on copying: OKX will then repeat CRYPTO NOVA's trades in your account automatically. An exchange is a marketplace where coins are bought and sold. Whether to repeat, copy or just watch is only your decision.
cards.example: In real life: an experienced gardener shows you how to prune an apple tree. You watch and do the same in your own garden — or decide to wait.

cards.title: Our advice for beginners
cards.text: Start with the lessons and a Piggy bank on the “Steady” strategy. For the first few weeks, just watch how the system trades on demo. Once you understand how stops and risk work, decide whether the active path is for you. Real money only if you're 18 or older, and only money you can spare.
cards.example: In real life: before buying a car, you take a test drive. One ride, and you already know whether it's the car for you.

lessons.title: Futures: how to read a trade
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to read a trade: where the entry, stop and target are, and why the system went in.

cards.title: Budget and result
cards.text: The “Futures” tab is the futures part of CRYPTO NOVA's real account on OKX. Its budget is 15% of the starting capital plus its own result. Leverage is 2x, with a cap of 3x. “Statistics” shows how many trades have closed and how many were in profit, and “Trade history” keeps every closed trade. The “largest drawdown” is the deepest fall from the highest point.
cards.example: In real life: a family keeps a separate envelope for the holiday. They spend from it, and whatever they win or lose stays in that same envelope.

cards.title: A trade in progress
cards.text: The “Open trades” block shows the trades in progress. For each one you can see the coin, the direction and the result in dollars. “Long” means the system expects the price to rise. “Short” means it expects the price to fall. If there are no trades, the system is waiting for a good entry point. That's normal.
cards.example: In real life: going long is like buying firewood in summer because you expect it to cost more by winter.

cards.title: The road from stop to target
cards.text: The price bar is like a road. At one end is the stop: if the price gets there, the trade closes with a small loss. At the other end is the target: that's where you take your profit. In between are the entry price and the “now” point. The closer the point is to the target, the better things are going.
cards.example: Example: entry $10, stop $9, target $13. At $11, the point is closer to the target, and the trade is in profit. At $9.50, the point is creeping toward the stop.

lessons.title: Spot and the Piggy bank: the calm path
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand how the “Spot” portfolio works and how to start a Piggy bank.

cards.title: Spot: coins without debt
cards.text: Spot means buying the coins themselves, with no leverage. Leverage is borrowed money used for a trade. There's no debt here: what you buy is what you hold. At the top is “Your portfolio”: what the set of coins is worth and how that has changed. A portfolio is everything your money is invested in.
cards.example: In real life: buying apples with your own money is relaxed. Buying them on credit is stressful: you have to repay the debt even if apples get cheaper.

cards.title: What's in the portfolio
cards.text: The “Allocation” block shows the shares. The core is bitcoin, ether, solana and other large coins. About 15% is kept in dollars as a reserve. Tap a coin and the app explains why it's in the portfolio: what the project is, its risks and its unlocks.
cards.example: In real life: you don't carry all your eggs in one basket. Drop one basket, and the eggs in the others are fine.

cards.title: The system keeps the balance
cards.text: Prices change, and the shares drift. The system sells some of what has grown a lot and buys more of what has shrunk. You can see its last action on the screen. In the “Demo calculation” block, you can enter your own amount, and the app will recalculate the portfolio for it.
cards.example: In real life: a gardener trims the branches that have grown too big and plants new ones where there's a gap. The garden stays even.

cards.title: Piggy bank: what for and how much
cards.text: The Piggy bank is a way to save in bitcoin, a little at a time. Step 1: what you're saving for — “Retirement”, “Kids' education” or “Dream” — and for how long. Step 2: the amount — $5, $10, $25 or $50, weekly or monthly. The app instantly shows how much you'll put aside.
cards.example: Example: $10 a week. In a year, that's $10 × 52 = $520 of your own contributions. In 10 years, $5,200.

cards.text: Step 3: the strategy. “Steady”: each time, we buy only bitcoin, with no leverage and no debt. It's the simplest path, and the one we recommend for beginners. “Active”: your Piggy bank goes into the system's spot portfolio. It holds more different coins, and the risk is higher.
cards.example: In real life: “Steady” is like dropping coins into a piggy bank. “Active” is like putting your money to work in a business: it may bring you more, or it may bring you less.

lessons.title: Safety: your money stays with you
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know how to protect your money and how to spot a scammer.

cards.title: Your money stays with you
cards.text: CRYPTO NOVA doesn't accept, hold or withdraw money. In demo, everything is for practice. Real money sits only in your exchange account. You deposit and withdraw it yourself, in the exchange app. We can't take even a cent from your account.
cards.example: In real life: a gym trainer suggests exercises, but the key to your locker stays with you.

cards.title: We don't need your exchange keys
cards.text: Right now, the app needs neither your exchange password nor an API key. An API key is a special pass that lets a program connect to an exchange. Copying CRYPTO NOVA doesn't need one either: you turn copying on in OKX itself. Never give anyone a key that can withdraw money.
cards.example: In real life: a mailbox key. You can use it to get your letters, but it won't open your front door.

cards.title: Passwords and your secret phrase are yours alone
cards.text: Never tell anyone your passwords, SMS codes or your wallet's secret phrase. The secret phrase, or seed phrase, is 12 or 24 words that open your wallet. CRYPTO NOVA will never ask for them. Anyone who does is a scammer.
cards.example: In real life: a real bank never asks for your card PIN over the phone.

cards.title: Fake “support”
cards.text: A scammer often messages you first and rushes you: “Urgent, or your account will be blocked!” They ask for a password, a code, or a money transfer “for verification.” They promise income with no risk. Always open our support yourself, from the app: “Account” → “Support”. Only use links to our website from the app itself.
cards.example: In real life: a “bank employee” calls and tries to scare you. A real bank doesn't do that. Hang up and call the bank yourself.

cards.title: NOVA is an assistant, not a fortune-teller
cards.text: NOVA explains trades and the market in plain words. But she's an AI, and she can be wrong. NOVA doesn't know your whole life: your debts, plans and savings. Her answers aren't financial advice. Don't send her passwords or personal details. In demo, you get 5 questions a day.
cards.example: In real life: a GPS shows you the way. But if it's steering you straight into a lake, you look at the road yourself.

cards.title: Simple rules for every day
cards.text: Start with demo and the lessons. Only invest money you can afford to lose. On the exchange, turn on sign-in with a code from your phone — that's two-factor protection. Check the website address. And don't rush: an honest offer won't vanish in 5 minutes.
cards.example: In real life: buckling up takes a second but protects you the whole way. These rules are the same kind of seatbelt for your money.

lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why the same amount of money buys a little less every year.

cards.title: Bread got more expensive
cards.text: Think back to what bread cost 10 years ago. Most likely, less than it does now. The same goes for bus fares and utility bills. Bread didn't get bigger or tastier — prices just creep up year after year. The chart shows real US data: what cost $100 in 2000 cost about $182 in 2024.
cards.example: In real life: Grandma says, “This money used to buy me a full bag of groceries.” And she's right.

chart.caption: US consumer price index (CPI-U, BLS): what cost $100 in 2000

cards.title: Same money, less to buy
cards.text: Say you have $100 and a loaf costs $2. That's enough for $100 ÷ $2 = 50 loaves. 5 years later, bread costs $2.50. Now $100 ÷ $2.50 = 40 loaves. Same bill, 10 fewer loaves.
cards.example: In real life: your paycheck stays the same, but your grocery bag gets lighter every year.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: how many loaves $100 buys

cards.title: This is called inflation
cards.text: When prices slowly rise and money buys less and less, that's called inflation. Prices usually rise by a few percent a year. Example: with 5% inflation, something that cost $100 costs $100 + 5% = $105 a year later.
cards.example: In real life: cash in a drawer is like ice in the sun. It just sits there quietly, but it buys less and less.

cards.title: Where it comes from
cards.text: Money is issued by the government through its central bank. If there's more money in the country but the same amount of goods, each bill is worth less. That's one of the main causes of inflation, but not the only one.
cards.example: In real life: a market has 10 watermelons and 10 buyers. Give every buyer twice as much money, and watermelons get pricier. After all, there aren't any more of them.

cards.title: How people protect their savings
cards.text: Money “under the mattress” quietly loses its power. That's why people keep savings in different ways: a bank deposit, gold, a home. More and more people add a little bitcoin too. Each option has its own risk, and none comes with a guarantee. So savings are often spread across several places.
cards.example: In real life: people pickle, dry and make jam from the harvest so it lasts until spring. Savings are kept in different ways for the same reason.

remember: Inflation: prices rise, and the same money buys less.
One cause: more money is printed while the amount of goods stays the same.
You can keep savings in different ways, but every way has risk.

quiz.q: You have $100. Bread went up from $2 to $2.50. How many loaves can you buy now?
quiz.why: $100 ÷ $2.50 = 40. Before, it was $100 ÷ $2 = 50. Same money, less bread — that's inflation.

quiz.q: What is inflation?
options: Shops run out of goods
Prices rise, and the same money buys less
The bank takes part of the money from your account
Salaries start being paid less often
quiz.why: Inflation is when prices rise little by little. The bill is the same, but it buys less.

quiz.q: Your money sits at home for a year, and inflation is 5%. What happens to it?
options: It grows by 5%
Nothing: it's worth just as much as a year ago
The bank takes it
You have the same number of bills, but they buy less
quiz.why: The number of bills doesn't change. But what cost $100 now costs $105, so the same money buys less.

lessons.title: What bitcoin is
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to explain to friends and family what bitcoin is and why people believe in it.

cards.title: Digital money with no owner
cards.text: Bitcoin is digital money. You can't touch it; it lives on the internet. The main difference from regular money: bitcoin has no owner. No bank or government controls it on its own. The rules are the same for everyone and are written into the program itself.
cards.example: In real life: regular money is like tap water — the owner controls the tap. Bitcoin is like a village well that everyone uses by shared rules.

cards.title: Who invented it
cards.text: Bitcoin appeared in 2009. It was created by a person or group of people using the name Satoshi Nakamoto. No one knows who that really is. Satoshi launched the system and disappeared. And bitcoin has been running without him for more than 17 years.
cards.example: In real life: someone made up the rules of a new game, shared them with everyone and walked away. The game goes on without them.

cards.title: Only 21,000,000 coins
cards.text: There will never be more than 21,000,000 bitcoins. That's been written into the rules from the very start. The 20-millionth bitcoin was created in March 2026. The last million will take more than 100 more years: about every 4 years, the issuance is cut in half. Ordinary money can be printed without limit, but bitcoin can't. That's why it's called “digital gold.”
cards.example: In real life: gold can't be printed either. It has to be mined, and there's only so much of it on Earth.

chart.caption: As of October 2026

cards.title: You can buy a small piece
cards.text: You don't need to buy a whole bitcoin. It splits into 100,000,000 tiny parts. The smallest part is called a “satoshi,” after its creator. As of 21.10.2026, 1 bitcoin cost about $83,000. But you can buy a piece of it for just a few dollars.
cards.example: In real life: you don't have to order a whole pizza. You can get a slice — it's from the same pizza.

cards.title: Why people believe in it
cards.text: Since January 2024, the US has had exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for bitcoin, since July 2024 for ether, and since autumn 2025 for other coins too. People buy them like ordinary stocks, and through them individuals, companies and big funds hold bitcoin. Financial companies are already issuing fund shares and bonds on the blockchain — this is called tokenization. Many see this as the start of crypto going mainstream.
cards.example: In real life: people used to go to the bank to buy a gold bar. Now they buy a share of a gold fund in an app. The same thing is happening with bitcoin.

cards.title: The honest truth about risk
cards.text: Bitcoin's price swings a lot. On 6 October 2025 it set a record of about $126,000, and in October 2026 it was worth roughly a third less. In the past, it has lost more than half its value several times, and then gone on to set new records. But the past doesn't promise the future. That's why sensible people only invest what they can afford to lose, and buy a little at a time.
cards.example: In real life: the sea can be calm or stormy. Anyone heading out to sea always takes a life jacket.

remember: Bitcoin is digital money with no owner, running since 2009.
There will never be more than 21,000,000 bitcoins.
The price swings a lot: only invest what you can afford to lose.

quiz.q: How many bitcoins can there be in total?
options: As many as a bank wants to print
No limit at all
quiz.why: The 21,000,000 limit has been in the rules from the start. And 100,000,000 is how many satoshis make up 1 bitcoin.

quiz.q: Can you buy less than 1 bitcoin?
options: Yes, bitcoin splits into small parts
No, it's only sold whole
Only if you take out a bank loan
Only once every 4 years
quiz.why: Bitcoin splits into 100,000,000 parts. So you can buy a piece even with a small amount.

quiz.q: Who controls bitcoin?
options: The US central bank
The company that issued it
Satoshi Nakamoto personally
No one on their own: the rules are the same for everyone
quiz.why: Bitcoin has no owner. The rules are written into the program, and thousands of computers around the world follow them.

lessons.title: Blockchain in plain words
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand how bitcoin works without a bank and why its records can't be faked.

cards.title: A shared notebook
cards.text: A blockchain is a big shared notebook where every bitcoin transfer is written down. “Anna sent Ben 1 bitcoin.” “Ben sent Chloe half of it.” From these lines, you can see who has how many coins.
cards.example: In real life: the tab book in a village shop, where the shopkeeper writes down who took what on credit. Only this notebook is one for the whole world.

cards.title: Copies with thousands of people
cards.text: This notebook isn't kept in one place. Exact copies of it sit on the computers of thousands of people around the world. Each new entry is added to all the copies at once. There's no master copy — all copies are equal.
cards.example: In real life: if someone loses their notebook, no problem. There are thousands of identical ones left.

cards.title: No secret edits
cards.text: Say someone secretly changes their copy: “I received 100 bitcoins.” Everyone else compares notebooks and sees that this copy doesn't match. The fake simply gets rejected.
cards.example: In real life: one witness might lie. But if 1,000 people saw the same thing, a lie gets spotted right away.

cards.title: Blocks and a chain
cards.text: Entries are gathered into pages called blocks. A new block appears about every 10 minutes: 60 ÷ 10 = 6 blocks an hour. Each block is firmly linked to the one before it, like links in a chain. Block + chain = blockchain.
cards.example: In real life: a notebook stitched together with thread. You can't tear out a page without anyone noticing — the thread breaks, and everyone sees it.

cards.title: Who keeps the records
cards.text: New blocks are added by powerful computers around the world. Their owners are called miners. They get new bitcoins for their work. Playing fair pays off for them: cheating would be spotted, and there'd be no reward.
cards.example: In real life: a cashier gets a bonus only if the till balances. If it doesn't, no bonus.

cards.title: The flip side
cards.text: This reliability comes at a price. A blockchain transfer can't be undone. Send it to the wrong person, and no one will give it back: there's no bank here. That's why the recipient's address — their wallet number — is always checked twice.
cards.example: In real life: once a letter drops into the mailbox, you can't get it back out.

remember: A blockchain is a shared notebook of transfers, copied by thousands of people.
A new block appears about every 10 minutes.
Entries can't be secretly changed, and transfers can't be undone.

quiz.q: Why is a blockchain entry hard to fake?
options: A big, reliable bank guards it
The notebook is hidden in a secret place
Thousands of people have copies, so a fake is easy to spot
Only one honest person makes the entries
quiz.why: A blockchain has no single keeper. Thousands of copies are checked against each other, and a copy that doesn't match gets rejected.

quiz.q: How often does a new block appear on the bitcoin network?
options: About once a day
About every 10 minutes
Every second
Once a month
quiz.why: About every 10 minutes. So about 60 ÷ 10 = 6 new blocks come out every hour.

quiz.q: You sent bitcoin to the wrong address. What will most likely happen?
options: You won't be able to get it back
The bank will cancel the transfer within 3 days
The coins will come back on their own in 10 minutes
Miners will return them if you file a request
quiz.why: Blockchain transfers can't be undone, and there's no bank to return the money. That's why addresses are always checked twice.

lessons.title: Why the price jumps around
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why bitcoin's price sometimes rises and sometimes falls.

cards.title: Apples in summer and winter
cards.text: In summer and fall, the market is piled high with apples. There are lots of sellers, and the price is low. In winter and spring, apples are scarce, but plenty of people want them. The price goes up. The chart shows the price of 1 kg of apples at different times of year.
cards.example: In real life: strawberries are cheap in June, but in January they cost as much as a gift.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: price of 1 kg of apples, $

cards.title: Supply and demand
cards.text: How many people want to buy is called demand. How much is up for sale is called supply. When more people want to buy than sell, the price rises. When more people want to sell than buy, the price falls. It works the same way with bitcoin.
cards.example: In real life: before Valentine's Day, everyone buys roses, and they get more expensive. The day after, there are plenty of roses and hardly any buyers.

cards.title: News
cards.text: News moves the price. Good news makes more people want to buy, and the price rises. Bad news makes many rush to sell, and the price falls. Sometimes bitcoin moves 5–10% in a single day. At a price of $80,000, that's up to $80,000 × 10% = $8,000.
cards.example: In real life: a rumor spreads that toilet paper will run out. Everyone rushes to stock up, and it gets pricier, even though the factory is working as usual.

cards.title: Fear and greed
cards.text: In the market, people are often driven by feelings. The price is rising — you want to buy so you don't miss out. That's greed. The price is falling — you want to sell everything right now. That's fear. Because of these feelings, the price often goes further than it “should.”
cards.example: In real life: a big sale. Everyone's grabbing things off the shelves, so you grab too — even though you only came in for bread.

cards.title: A roller coaster
cards.text: That's why bitcoin's chart looks like a roller coaster. And there's some important math here. If the price drops 50%, it needs to rise 100% to get back. Example: $100 − 50% = $50. To turn $50 back into $100, you need +100%.
cards.example: In real life: going down a hill is quick, but climbing back up is long and hard.

chart.caption: Illustrative example

remember: More people want to buy than sell — the price rises.
News, fear and greed make the price swing hard.
Down 50%? It takes a 100% rise to get back.

quiz.q: There are suddenly many more people buying bitcoin, but no more sellers. What will most likely happen to the price?
options: The price will fall
The price won't change
The price will rise
The exchange will stop trading
quiz.why: More people want to buy than sell — the price rises. Like roses before Valentine's Day. But that's “most likely,” not a promise.

quiz.q: The price fell from $100 to $50. How much does it need to rise to get back to $100?
options: By 50%
By 25%
quiz.why: $50 + 50% = $75 — not enough. But $50 + 100% = $100. That's why it's so hard to recover after a big drop.

quiz.q: The price is shooting up, and everyone around you is buying. What feeling most often pushes people to buy?
options: Greed: the fear of missing out on a profit
Fear of losing money
Calm calculation
Boredom
quiz.why: When everyone's buying, you don't want to be left behind. That's greed. Fear works the other way: it pushes people to sell when the price falls.

lessons.title: Market cap: why a «cheap» coin isn't cheap
lessons.goal: After this lesson you'll see what a coin is really worth and won't fall for «cheap» coins that cost a fraction of a cent.

cards.title: The price of one coin says nothing
cards.text: Every coin has its own number of units. One has 20 M, another has a trillion. So the price of one coin on its own doesn't tell you if it's expensive or cheap.
cards.example: In real life: a $10 pizza costs the same whether you cut it into 8 slices or 100. The slice is cheaper — the pizza is the same.

cards.title: Market cap = price × number of coins
cards.text: To see what the whole coin is worth, multiply the price by the number of coins in circulation. That's the market cap. Bitcoin in October 2026: about $83 000 × about 20 M coins ≈ $1.66 trillion. The chart shows two coins: «cheap» A at $0.001 and «expensive» B at $50.
cards.example: In real life: a $1 share isn't necessarily cheaper than a $500 share. What matters is what the whole company is worth.

chart.caption: Market cap, $ M. «Cheap» A is worth twice as much as B

cards.title: The «cheap coin» trap
cards.text: «A $0.001 coin will surely reach $1» is a common dream. That's a 1 000× rise. If there are 1 trillion of those coins, at $1 the whole coin would be worth $1 trillion — almost as much as all of bitcoin. Work out the market cap and the fairy tale shows.
cards.example: In real life: «a flat for just $1 000» — you check and it's the price per square metre, not for the whole flat.

cards.title: Future coins: FDV
cards.text: Some coins haven't been released yet and will come out later. Price × all coins, including future ones, is FDV, the fully diluted value. If FDV is much bigger than the market cap, new coins will be sold bit by bit, and that weighs on the price. Both numbers are on CoinMarketCap and CoinGecko.
cards.example: In real life: a company announces it will issue as many shares again. Your share of it gets smaller.

remember: The price of one coin on its own doesn't say if it's expensive or cheap.
Market cap = price × number of coins in circulation.
If many more coins are still to come (FDV much bigger), that weighs on the price.

quiz.q: Coin A costs $0.001 and there are 1 trillion of them. Coin B costs $50 and there are 10 M of them. Which has the bigger market cap?
options: A: $1 billion
B: $500 million
They're equal
It can't be worked out

quiz.q: How is market cap calculated?
options: Price × number of coins in circulation
Price ÷ number of coins
Trading volume over a day
It's the price of one coin
quiz.why: Market cap is the price of one coin times the number of coins in circulation. It shows what the whole coin is worth.

quiz.q: A coin costs $0.01 and there are 100 billion of them. What would its market cap be if the price reached $1?
options: $1 billion
$10 billion
$100 billion
$1 trillion
quiz.why: 100 000 000 000 × $1 = $100 billion. Today it's 100 billion × $0.01 = $1 billion — so it would need to grow 100×.

lessons.title: Where people buy crypto: the exchange
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know where and how people buy bitcoin, and what it costs.

cards.title: An exchange is like a market
cards.text: Most people buy crypto on an exchange. An exchange is a website or app where some people sell coins and others buy them. It's like a currency exchange booth: you hand over dollars and get bitcoin.
cards.example: In real life: before a trip abroad, you swap dollars for euros at an exchange booth. On a crypto exchange, you swap dollars for bitcoin.

cards.title: First, sign up
cards.text: To buy on an exchange, you need a personal page — an account. Usually you're asked for an email, a phone number and an ID document to confirm who you are. This protects against scammers. You can only buy with real money if you're 18 or older.
cards.example: In real life: a bank won't open an account for you without ID either.

cards.title: A piece for $10
cards.text: You don't need to buy a whole bitcoin. Say 1 bitcoin costs $80,000 and you have $10. Let's do the math: $10 ÷ $80,000 = 0.000125 bitcoin. It's not much, but it's a real piece of bitcoin. Its price moves along with bitcoin's.
cards.example: In real life: you don't have to buy the whole cake. You can get a slice — it's from the same cake.

cards.title: Fees
cards.text: For every purchase and sale, the exchange charges a small fee. It's often a fraction of a percent. Example: a 0.1% fee. You buy $100 worth and pay $100 × 0.1% = $0.10. Buying with a bank card can cost more.
cards.example: In real life: an exchange booth makes money too — it sells dollars for a bit more than it buys them for.

cards.title: Where your coins are kept
cards.text: Coins you buy on an exchange sit in your account on that exchange. It's convenient, but you're trusting the company with them. If the exchange gets hacked or shuts down, you could lose your money. That's why people choose big exchanges and turn on sign-in with a code from their phone.
cards.example: In real life: money in a bank is convenient, but you're trusting the bank. An exchange is similar, except there's usually no government deposit insurance.

cards.title: Practice first
cards.text: Before spending real money, you can practice. CRYPTO NOVA has a demo account: virtual money and real prices. Mistakes there cost nothing. And the Piggy bank will show you how regular purchases work.
cards.example: In real life: before driving in the city, you learn on the driving school's practice lot.

remember: An exchange is a market where regular money is swapped for crypto.
You can buy a piece of bitcoin, for example for $10.
Exchanges charge fees; real money is for 18+ only.

quiz.q: You have $10, and 1 bitcoin costs $80,000. Can you buy bitcoin?
options: No, first you need to save up for a whole one
Only if you take out a loan
Only on a demo account
Yes, you can buy a small piece of it
quiz.why: $10 ÷ $80,000 = 0.000125 bitcoin. That's a real piece of bitcoin, and its price moves along with it.

quiz.q: The exchange fee is 0.1%. You buy $200 worth. How much goes to the fee?
quiz.why: $200 × 0.1% = $0.20. An easy way to remember it: 0.1% is 10 cents for every $100.

quiz.q: From what age can you buy crypto on an exchange with real money?
options: From 18
From 14
From 16
At any age
quiz.why: Real money and exchanges are for adults only, 18 and up. You can learn on a demo account, without real money.

lessons.title: Wallets and keys
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know how to store crypto and how not to lose access to it.

cards.title: There are no coins in a wallet
cards.text: A crypto wallet is an app, or a small device that looks like a USB stick. Surprisingly, there are no coins inside. They're recorded on the blockchain. The wallet holds a key — your access to your coins.
cards.example: In real life: your money sits in a bank safe-deposit box, and all you have in your pocket is the key to it.

cards.title: The key is both a safe and a password
cards.text: A key is like a safe key and a password rolled into one. Whoever knows the key owns the coins. Without the key, even you can't use them. And with the key, anyone can take them.
cards.example: In real life: if a thief learns the code to your safe, he doesn't need your ID. He just opens the door.

cards.title: Seed phrase: 12 or 24 words
cards.text: The main key is usually written down as 12 or 24 simple words, most often in English. This is called a seed phrase, or secret phrase. It's called a “seed” because all your keys grow from it. With these words, you can restore the wallet on any phone.
cards.example: In real life: it's the spare key to your home. Lose your phone, and the words get you back in on a new one.

cards.title: Lose it, and it's gone
cards.text: If both your phone and your seed phrase are lost, the coins are gone forever. No bank, no support, no “Forgot password?” button. There are plenty of stories of people losing large sums this way.
cards.example: In real life: the key to your safe falls into a river, and there's no spare. The money is inside, but nobody can ever open the safe.

cards.title: Never show it to anyone
cards.text: Never tell anyone your seed phrase: not “support,” not a friend, not a website. An honest service will never ask for it. Write it down on paper and keep it somewhere safe at home. Don't take photos of it or send it to anyone.
cards.example: In real life: you wouldn't tell your card PIN even to a polite voice “from the bank.” A seed phrase is the same, only even stricter.

cards.title: Exchange or your own wallet
cards.text: On an exchange, the company manages the keys: it's convenient, but you're trusting them. In your own wallet, only you have the keys: everything is in your hands, and so is all the responsibility. The choice depends on what you trust more.
cards.example: In real life: you can keep money in a bank or in a safe at home. In the bank, others guard it for you; at home, you guard it yourself.

remember: A wallet doesn't hold coins — it holds the key to them.
A 12- or 24-word seed phrase is the master key: lose it, and it's gone for good.
Never show your seed phrase to anyone, even “support.”

quiz.q: What does a crypto wallet actually hold?
options: The coins themselves, like bills in a wallet
A copy of your passport
A key that gives access to the coins
Your bank card number
quiz.why: The coins are recorded on the blockchain. The wallet holds the key to them, and whoever knows the key owns the coins.

quiz.q: “Customer support” messages you and asks for your seed phrase to “protect your account.” What should you do?
options: Tell them — it's support, after all
Tell them nothing: it's scammers
Tell them only half the words
Send a photo of the paper with the words
quiz.why: Real support never asks for your seed phrase. Even some of the words help a thief. Just end the conversation.

quiz.q: The phone with your wallet is lost, but your seed phrase is written down at home. What happens?
options: You can restore the wallet on a new phone
The coins are gone forever
You have to go to the bank for a new key
The coins go to whoever found the phone
quiz.why: The seed phrase is your spare key. With these words, you can restore the wallet on any phone. That's exactly why it's kept so carefully.

lessons.title: Stablecoins: digital dollars
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand what USDT and USDC are, why they're needed, and what their risks are.

cards.title: A coin that doesn't jump
cards.text: Bitcoin's price swings a lot. But sometimes you need digital money that holds steady, like a dollar. That's what stablecoins were invented for. The name says it all: they're meant to be stable.
cards.example: In real life: market prices change, but a 1 kg weight on a scale always weighs 1 kg. A stablecoin tries to always “weigh” $1.

cards.title: USDT and USDC
cards.text: The best-known stablecoins are USDT and USDC. Each of these coins aims to be worth $1. Example: 100 USDT is about $100 today, tomorrow and a month from now. As long as everything goes as usual.
cards.example: In real life: it's like a dollar, except it lives in your phone instead of your wallet.

cards.title: Who issues them
cards.text: Stablecoins are issued by companies, not governments. USDT is issued by a company called Tether, and USDC by a company called Circle. They promise that for every coin, they hold $1 in reserve. You're trusting that promise.
cards.example: In real life: a coat-check ticket. On its own, it's just a scrap of paper. It's valuable because your coat is hanging behind it.

cards.title: There's still risk
cards.text: A stablecoin isn't a dollar in your pocket. The company could make mistakes or get into trouble. It can freeze coins if the authorities demand it. Stablecoins have dropped below $1 before, and some have lost their value entirely. There are no guarantees.
cards.example: In real life: a coat-check ticket works only while the cloakroom is open. Once it closes, the ticket won't get you anything.

cards.title: Rules for stablecoins
cards.text: Governments have taken on stablecoins. In July 2025 the US passed the GENIUS Act: the reserve must be held 1:1 in dollars and short-term US Treasury bills, and a report on it must come out every month. In the EU the MiCA rules apply: exchanges with an EU licence don't sell stablecoins that lack authorization, such as USDT. There, people use USDC and euro stablecoins. This is as of October 2026.
cards.example: In real life: the cloakroom used to run on trust. Now an inspector comes by and counts the coats on the hangers.

cards.title: Why they're useful
cards.text: On an exchange, a stablecoin works like a “dollar wallet.” You sell bitcoin, get USDT, and wait calmly. When you want to buy again, you pay with the same USDT. You don't have to move money back to the bank every time.
cards.example: In real life: on a trip, you keep some money in the local currency. That way you don't have to run to an exchange booth every time.

cards.title: A reserve in the portfolio
cards.text: Keeping part of your money in dollars is like a rainy-day fund. For example, the CRYPTO NOVA spot portfolio keeps about 15% in dollars. When the market falls, the dollar part barely changes. And you can use it to buy more coins at a lower price.
cards.example: In real life: an umbrella in your bag won't stop the rain, but it helps you wait it out.

chart.caption: CRYPTO NOVA spot portfolio, October 2026

remember: USDT and USDC aim to always be worth $1.
They're issued by companies — so there's risk.
On an exchange, a stablecoin is a handy “dollar wallet.”

quiz.q: How much does 1 USDT aim to be worth?
options: The same as bitcoin
A different amount every day
quiz.why: USDT and USDC are stablecoins. They aim to always be worth $1, which is why they're called digital dollars.

quiz.q: Who issues USDT and USDC?
options: The US central bank
Bitcoin miners
The BingX exchange
Private companies
quiz.why: USDT is issued by Tether, and USDC by Circle. You're trusting their promise to hold reserves, so there's risk.

quiz.q: Why is a stablecoin useful on an exchange?
options: To keep your money in “dollars” between purchases
To make sure the price goes up
To never pay fees
To get leverage
quiz.why: You sell bitcoin, get USDT, and wait. It doesn't have to grow: its job is to stay at $1.

lessons.title: Scammers: 7 warning signs
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll recognize a scam by 7 signs and know what to do.

cards.title: Where there's money, there are thieves
cards.text: Crypto has lots of scammers. They like that transfers can't be undone. The good news: almost all scams look alike. Learn these 7 signs, and you'll be very hard to fool.
cards.example: In real life: a call “from the bank”: “Someone is taking money from your card, tell us the code right now.” Crypto scams use the same trick.

cards.title: Signs 1–2: no risk, and hurry
cards.text: 1. They promise big income with no risk. That doesn't exist: where there's income, there's risk. 2. They rush you: “today only,” “just 3 spots left.” The rush is there so you don't have time to think or ask anyone for advice.
cards.example: In real life: a street seller whispers, “Grab it quick — last one, half price.” The harder they push, the more carefully you should look.

cards.title: Signs 3–4: passwords and “support”
cards.text: 3. They ask for your seed phrase, a password or an SMS code. An honest service never asks for these. 4. “Support” messages you first on a messaging app or social media. Real support doesn't do that: you contact them yourself, from the app or the website.
cards.example: In real life: a stranger at your door says he's from the gas company and asks for your house keys.

cards.title: Signs 5–7: “we'll double it,” fake sites, celebrities
cards.text: 5. “Send us 1 bitcoin and we'll send back 2.” You'll get nothing back. 6. Fake websites: the address is off by 1 letter, but the site looks like the real thing. 7. “A celebrity is giving away crypto.” The videos, photos and even the voice are faked with AI, and the star knows nothing about it.
cards.example: In real life: a letter says, “You've won $1,000,000! Just pay for shipping.” There's no such thing as a free lunch.

cards.title: What to do
cards.text: If in doubt, stop and don't send anything. Close the chat. Open the exchange website yourself, from a bookmark. Talk it over with someone close to you. If you've already sent something, change your passwords and contact the real support team and the police.
cards.example: In real life: someone calls “from the bank”? Hang up and dial the number on the back of your card yourself.

remember: Income with no risk, pressure to hurry, a request for your seed phrase — that's a scam.
Support never messages first; “we'll double your bitcoin” is always a lie.
If in doubt, stop and don't send anything.

quiz.q: An “exchange manager” messages you: “Your account is at risk, tell us the SMS code right now.” What is this?
options: A routine security check
The exchange looking out for your account
A scammer: they messaged first, they're rushing you, and they want a code
A new exchange rule
quiz.why: There are 3 signs here at once: they messaged first, they're rushing you, and they're asking for a code. Real support doesn't do that. Close the chat.

quiz.q: A website promises 5% a day with no risk at all. How should you treat it?
options: It's a sign of a scam: there's no income without risk
You could try it with a small amount
If the site looks good and has reviews, you can trust it
You need to invest while the offer lasts
quiz.why: Where there's income, there's risk. A “no risk” promise is the biggest sign of a scam. Even a small amount most likely won't come back.

quiz.q: A video: a famous businessman is giving away bitcoin. “Send 0.1 and get 0.2 back.” What should you do?
options: Send a little to test it
Send it, since he's famous
Forward it to friends so they don't miss out
Send nothing: it's a scam
quiz.why: There are 2 signs here at once: “we'll double it” and “a celebrity is giving it away.” The video is fake, and whatever you send won't come back.

lessons.title: Ether and smart contracts
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will understand how ether differs from bitcoin and what a smart contract is.

cards.title: Ether is more than a coin
cards.text: Ethereum (ether, ETH) launched in 2015. As of October 2026, it's the second-largest cryptocurrency after bitcoin. Bitcoin mostly stores and moves money, while the Ethereum network also runs programs.
cards.example: In real life: bitcoin is a reliable safe, ether is a safe with automation that opens by itself when a condition is met.

cards.title: A smart contract
cards.text: A smart contract is a program on a blockchain that follows the rule «if A happens, do B». It cannot be quietly rewritten afterwards, and it works without a middleman. Coin swaps, loans and stablecoins run on smart contracts.
cards.example: In real life: a vending machine. Drop a coin, get water. No shop assistant needed.

cards.title: Gas is the fee for an action
cards.text: Every action on the Ethereum network costs a small fee called gas. It is paid in ether to those who keep the network running. When many people use the network, gas gets pricier; when few do, it gets cheaper.
cards.example: In real life: a taxi costs more at rush hour and less at night.

cards.title: Risks
cards.text: Smart-contract code can contain bugs, and money has been stolen through them more than once. Ether's price usually swings harder than bitcoin's. So start small and use only well-known services.
cards.example: In real life: even a good lock can be faulty. That is why big sums are not kept where you are unsure.

remember: Ether is a network for programs, not just a coin.
A smart contract carries out an «if — then» rule by itself, without a middleman.
Actions on the network cost gas; code can contain bugs.

quiz.q: What is a smart contract?
options: A paper agreement at a notary
A program on a blockchain that carries out a condition by itself
A bank loan
An exchange app
quiz.why: A smart contract is a program following «if A — then B». It runs by itself, without a middleman.

quiz.q: What is gas on the Ethereum network?
options: Fuel for servers
The fee for an action on the network
The name of a wallet
A type of stablecoin
quiz.why: Gas is the fee for each action on the network. It goes to those who keep the network running.

quiz.q: Which risk of smart contracts is real?
options: A bug in the code through which money is stolen
The contract does not work at night
The contract works in one country only
There is no risk
quiz.why: Code is written by people and can contain bugs. Large sums have already been stolen through them.

lessons.title: Fees: what a purchase really costs
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will be able to add up every cost of buying and withdrawing crypto.

cards.title: The exchange fee
cards.text: The exchange takes a percentage of every trade. Often it is 0.1%: buy $100 — pay $100 × 0.1% = $0.10. On small sums it is pennies, but with frequent trades it adds up noticeably.
cards.example: In real life: a bank transfer fee. Once it is unnoticeable, every day it is real money.

chart.caption: What a 0.1% fee costs on $100 trades, $

cards.title: The spread
cards.text: The buying price and the selling price on an exchange differ slightly. This gap is called the spread. For popular coins it is tiny, for rare ones it is noticeable: buy and sell right away — and you are already down.
cards.example: In real life: an exchange booth buys dollars cheaper than it sells them.

cards.title: The network fee for withdrawals
cards.text: When you withdraw coins from the exchange to your own wallet, you pay a network fee. It is usually a fixed amount, not a percentage: withdrawing $20 or $2,000 costs the same. So withdrawing in small bits does not pay.
cards.example: In real life: shipping a parcel costs the same whatever is inside.

cards.title: Count honestly
cards.text: Before a trade, add everything up: the exchange fee, the spread and the withdrawal fee. Buy $100 and sell right away at 0.1% per trade — that is already −$0.20, plus the spread. Profit is what is left after all costs.
cards.example: In real life: a bargain in another city is counted together with the trip.

remember: The exchange takes a percentage of every trade.
The spread is the gap between the buying and the selling price.
Withdrawals cost a fixed fee: withdraw less often and in bigger amounts.

quiz.q: The fee is 0.1%. You buy $500. How much do you pay?
What is the spread?
options: A crypto tax
The gap between the buying price and the selling price
A withdrawal fee
The name of a stablecoin
quiz.why: The spread is the difference between the price you can buy at and the price you can sell at.

quiz.q: Why is withdrawing coins in small parts a bad deal?
options: The network fee is fixed and eats a large share of a small amount
The exchange forbids it
The coins get lost
Withdrawals cost nothing
quiz.why: The withdrawal fee is usually the same. A $5 fee is 25% of $20 but 0.25% of $2,000.

lessons.title: Protecting your account: password and two-factor check
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will know how to protect an exchange account in 10 minutes.

cards.title: One password — one site
cards.text: If your email password also opens the exchange, a leak on one site opens them all. The exchange needs its own long password. A password manager makes storing passwords easy.
cards.example: In real life: nobody makes one key for the flat, the car and the safe.

cards.title: Two-factor check (2FA)
cards.text: Besides the password you need a code from an authenticator app on your phone. Even if the password is stolen, nobody can log in without the phone. SMS codes are weaker: fraudsters sometimes get a copy of someone else's SIM card.
cards.example: In real life: a door with two locks — one key in your pocket, the other in your phone.

cards.title: Backup codes
cards.text: When you turn on 2FA, the exchange gives you backup codes. Write them on paper and keep them somewhere safe. If you lose your phone, they get you back in.
cards.example: In real life: a spare key goes to a relative, not under the doormat.

cards.title: Who never gets your codes
cards.text: Exchange staff and «support» never ask for a 2FA code, a password or a wallet phrase. Whoever asks is a fraudster, even if they write in the exchange's name and with its logo.
cards.example: In real life: a bank never calls to ask for your PIN.

remember: The exchange gets its own long password.
Turn on 2FA with an authenticator app.
Codes and passwords go to no one — not even «support».

quiz.q: What does 2FA give you?
options: Faster trades
Without the second code from your phone nobody can log in, even with the password
Lower fees
Nothing
quiz.why: 2FA is a second lock. A stolen password is not enough: the code from your phone is needed too.

quiz.q: «Exchange support» asks for the code from your authenticator. What do you do?
options: Give the code
Send the password instead
Give nothing: it is a fraudster
Send the wallet phrase
quiz.why: Real support never asks for codes or passwords. Such a request is always fraud.

quiz.q: Where should you keep 2FA backup codes?
options: In notes on the same phone
On paper in a safe place
In a chat with friends
Nowhere, they are not needed
quiz.why: If the phone is lost, the notes on it are lost too. Paper in a safe place is the simplest way.

lessons.title: AI fakes: voices, faces and videos
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to spot a fake made with AI and know how to check it.

cards.title: Scams got smarter
cards.text: Scammers now use AI. It fakes the voices, faces and videos of people you know and of celebrities, and writes smooth messages with no mistakes. According to Chainalysis, scammers took about $17 billion in crypto in 2025. And cases where they pretend to be someone else became about 15 times more common.
cards.example: In real life: a fake used to give itself away with clumsy handwriting. Now a signature can be faked so well you can't tell by eye.

cards.title: What it looks like
cards.text: A video: a famous businessman “gives away” bitcoin or praises a platform paying 3% a day. A voice message from your “son”: “Mom, send money right now.” A video call from an “exchange employee” with the real logo. A fake like this takes a few minutes to make.
cards.example: Example: an ad on social media where a news anchor “recommends” a new crypto platform. The anchor is real, but the words were generated by AI.

cards.title: A one-minute check
cards.text: Don't trust your eyes and ears — check the channel. Hang up and call back yourself on a number you know. Ask a question only the real person can answer. Agree on a code word with your family. Open websites yourself, from a bookmark, not from a link in a video.
cards.example: In real life: a courier says he's from the bank. You don't argue with him — you just call the bank yourself.

cards.title: The main sign hasn't changed
cards.text: The technology is new, but the scheme is old: rushing you, income with no risk, and a request to send money or share a code. If you see that, it's a scam, however real the video looks. CRYPTO NOVA doesn't call you, doesn't ask you to send money and doesn't ask for codes.
cards.example: In real life: a fake banknote can look beautiful. But if someone is rushing to pay with it in the dark, be on your guard.

remember: AI fakes voices, faces and videos — you can't trust your eyes and ears.
Check it yourself: call back, ask the code word, open the site from a bookmark.
Rushing, income with no risk, a request to send money — it's a scam.

quiz.q: You get a voice message: your son's voice asks you to urgently send $500 in crypto. What do you do first?
options: Send it: that's definitely his voice
Send half
Hang up and call your son back yourself on his number
Ask him to send a photo
quiz.why: A voice can be faked in minutes, and so can a photo. The check is simple: call back yourself on a number you know.

quiz.q: A video: a celebrity recommends a platform paying 3% a day. How should you treat it?
options: It's a scam: the video is fake, and there's no income without risk
You could invest a little
If a celebrity recommends it, it must be safe
Forward it to friends
quiz.why: There are 2 signs at once: “a star recommends it” and huge income with no risk. Videos like this are often made with AI.

quiz.q: What helps a family avoid falling for a faked voice?
options: Answering every call
Agreeing on a code word and calling back yourself
Keeping passwords in your notes
Turning off the internet
quiz.why: Only your own people know the code word. And when you call back on a known number, you reach the real person.

lessons.title: How to withdraw money from an exchange
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know how to get money from an exchange back to your card without making mistakes on a transfer.

cards.title: Only you withdraw
cards.text: The money in your exchange account is yours. You withdraw it yourself, in the exchange app. CRYPTO NOVA can't withdraw it and doesn't ask for withdrawal access. Before a withdrawal, the exchange may ask for a code from an app or an SMS — that protects your account.
cards.example: In real life: only you can take cash from an ATM — with your card and your PIN.

cards.title: To your card: 3 steps
cards.text: Step 1: sell your coins for dollars — USDT or USDC. Step 2: choose a withdrawal to a card or a bank account. Exchanges do this through partners, and the buttons have different names. Step 3: check the amount, the fee and the timing. The money usually arrives within a few minutes to a few days.
cards.example: In real life: when travelling, you first change money at an exchange office, then take out cash. Same here: dollars first, then the card.

cards.title: Sending to a wallet: network and address
cards.text: You can also send coins to your own wallet or another exchange. Two things matter here: the network and the address. The sender's and the receiver's network must match. Copy the address instead of typing it, and check the first and last characters. A mistaken transfer is almost impossible to get back.
cards.example: Example: you're sending 100 USDT to a new address. First, a test transfer of 5 USDT. Once it arrives, send the other 95.

cards.title: Fees and taxes
cards.text: Withdrawals have fees. Sending coins costs a fixed network fee; a card withdrawal costs a percentage to the exchange's partner. So withdraw less often and in bigger amounts. In many countries, selling coins is the moment when tax is calculated. Keep your exchange statement.
cards.example: In real life: one big trip to the shop is cheaper than ten small ones.

remember: You withdraw money yourself, in the exchange app.
To a card: sell for dollars → withdraw → check the fee.
When sending coins, check the network and address, and start with a small amount.

quiz.q: Who can withdraw money from your exchange account?
options: CRYPTO NOVA
Only you
Anyone who knows your UID
“Support” from a messenger app
quiz.why: Only you make withdrawals, in the exchange app. Your UID number gives no access to the money.

quiz.q: You're sending USDT to a new address for the first time. What's sensible?
options: Send everything at once
Type the address by hand
Send a small amount first and check it
Pick any network
quiz.why: A test transfer checks both the address and the network. A mistaken transfer is almost impossible to get back.

quiz.q: Why is it cheaper to withdraw less often and in bigger amounts?
options: Withdrawals have fees, and small withdrawals eat up more
Bitcoin grows faster that way
The exchange bans small withdrawals
It makes no difference
quiz.why: The network fee is fixed, and card withdrawals take a percentage. Ten small withdrawals usually cost more than one.

levels.level_sub: How to save and grow your money calmly over the years, without fuss or panic

lessons.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why it's worth holding several coins plus a reserve in dollars.

cards.title: Old wisdom
cards.text: Grandmas say: don't put all your eggs in one basket. Drop the basket, and they all break. Spread them across three, and only some get hurt. Money works the same way. This is called diversification. It's a fancy word, but the idea is simple: don't bet everything on one thing.
cards.example: In real life: gardeners don't plant only potatoes — they plant carrots and onions too. If hail ruins the potatoes, there's still a harvest.

cards.title: One coin, one big risk
cards.text: Say all your money is in one coin. And then something goes wrong with it: a hack or a scandal. Its price falls to a fifth of what it was — and so does your money. But if that coin was just one part of your portfolio, the loss is smaller. Your portfolio is everything you've put your money into.
cards.example: Example: $1,000 in one coin, and its price falls to a fifth: $1,000 ÷ 5 = $200. But if it held only $100 of your $1,000, you lose $80, not $800.

cards.title: What a portfolio might look like
cards.text: The core is usually the biggest coins, like bitcoin and ether. A few others are added to them. And part is kept in dollars as a reserve. A portfolio like this swings less than a single coin. This is an example, not advice on what to buy.
cards.example: In real life: your closet has a warm jacket, an umbrella and a T-shirt. Whatever the weather, you've got something for it.

chart.caption: Illustrative example

cards.title: Why keep a reserve in dollars
cards.text: Dollars barely change in price. When the market falls, this part stays put. And you can use it to buy more coins at a lower price. In crypto, these “dollars” are usually stablecoins, like USDT. They aim to be worth $1, but they're issued by companies, so they carry risk too.
cards.example: In real life: a spare fuel can in the trunk. While all is well, it just sits there. But at the right moment, it's a lifesaver.

cards.title: Honestly: baskets don't protect you from everything
cards.text: In crypto, coins often fall together. When bitcoin falls, almost everything usually falls with it. So holding several coins lowers your risk, but doesn't remove it. A dollar reserve softens the blow, but it doesn't make investing safe either.
cards.example: In real life: an umbrella doesn't stop the rain. But under an umbrella, you get a lot less wet.

cards.title: How it works in CRYPTO NOVA
cards.text: In the “Spot” section, the system holds a portfolio of several coins: bitcoin, ether, solana and other major ones. About 15% sits in dollars as a reserve. When the shares get out of balance, the system sells what's grown too big and buys more of what has shrunk.
cards.example: In real life: a gardener trims branches that have grown too big and plants new ones where there's a gap. The garden stays even.

remember: Don't keep all your money in one coin.
A dollar reserve softens drops and gives you money to buy more.
Several coins lower the risk, but don't remove it completely.

quiz.q: What does “don't put all your eggs in one basket” mean for investing?
options: Buy one coin, the most reliable one
Spread your money across different coins and a reserve
Buy coins every day
Keep all your money in dollars only
quiz.why: When your money is spread out, trouble with one coin takes only a part, not everything.

quiz.q: You have $1,000. One coin holds $100 of it, and its price falls to a fifth. How much have you lost if the rest hasn't changed?
quiz.why: $100 ÷ 5 = $20. It was $100, now it's $20 — a loss of $80. The other $900 are fine.

quiz.q: Why can even a portfolio of 5 coins drop sharply?
options: Crypto coins often fall together
5 coins is too few
The dollar reserve also halves in value
It can't: a portfolio protects you completely
quiz.why: When bitcoin falls, almost the whole market usually falls with it. Baskets lower the risk, but they don't cancel it.

lessons.title: Piggy bank: buy a little, regularly
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why small regular purchases are calmer than one big one.

cards.title: Timing the market is almost impossible
cards.text: Many people wait for the lowest price to buy. But no one knows it in advance — not a beginner, not a pro. The price may drop even lower. Or it may climb while you wait. There's a simpler way: don't guess — buy a little at a time, regularly.
cards.example: In real life: no one knows which day cucumbers will be cheapest at the market. But if you buy every week, on average it works out fine.

cards.title: How the Piggy bank works
cards.text: You choose an amount and how often to buy. For example, $10 every week. And you buy on that day, whatever the price. No news, no worry. This is called averaging: you end up paying an average price — not the lowest, but not the highest either.
cards.example: That's how the “Piggy bank” works in CRYPTO NOVA: from $5 to $50, weekly or monthly. It reminds you on buy day.

cards.title: Cheaper means more coins
cards.text: Here's the Piggy bank's main secret. When the price is low, the same amount gets you more coins. When it's high, fewer. So it happens on its own: you get more when it's cheap and less when it's expensive. And a price drop isn't so scary anymore: it's like a sale.
cards.example: Say a coin costs $10: $50 ÷ $10 = 5 coins. A week later, it costs $5: $50 ÷ $5 = 10 coins. A week after that, it's $10 again: 5 coins again.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: how many coins $50 buys

cards.title: Simple math
cards.text: Over 3 weeks, you put in $50 × 3 = $150. You got 5 + 10 + 5 = 20 coins. Average price: $150 ÷ 20 = $7.50. If you'd bought everything at once in the first week, you'd have $150 ÷ $10 = 15 coins. Buying regularly got you 5 more coins.
cards.example: To be honest: if the price only ever goes up, buying everything at once works out better. The Piggy bank doesn't always win. But it takes away the guessing and the stress.

cards.title: What happened in the past
cards.text: We tested the Piggy bank on real bitcoin prices with a 0.1% fee: the same amount every week. At prices as of October 19, 2026, every $100 put aside would have turned into about $115 over 3 years, and about $191 over 5 years. That's how it went in the past — there are no guarantees.
cards.example: Example: $10 a week for 5 years is 261 purchases, or $2,610 of your own money. It would have become about $2,610 × 1.91 ≈ $4,985.

cards.title: Honestly: it's been in the red too
cards.text: Time matters a lot. Over 2 years, the Piggy bank was in the red: every $100 became $96. And over 5 years, there was a moment when it was worth 49% less than what had been put in — almost half. Those who got scared and sold were left with a loss. Those who kept going had almost doubled their money by October 19, 2026. There's no guarantee it will happen again.
cards.example: In real life: a tree takes years to grow. If you dig it up every month to check the roots, it never will.

chart.caption: What every $100 in a bitcoin Piggy bank would have become, as of October 19, 2026. The past, not a promise

remember: No need to time the market: the same amount, on a schedule.
When the price is lower, the same amount buys more coins.
In the past, the Piggy bank has been both up and down. There are no guarantees.

quiz.q: A coin costs $5. How many coins do you get for $50?
quiz.why: $50 ÷ $5 = 10 coins. The lower the price, the more coins you get for the same amount.

quiz.q: What's the main idea behind the Piggy bank?
options: Buy only when the price hits rock bottom
Put everything in at once and forget about it
Sell every time the price falls
Buy the same amount regularly, without trying to time the market
quiz.why: No one knows where the bottom is in advance. Regular buying takes away the guessing: you get more when it's cheap and less when it's expensive.

quiz.q: When tested on past prices, the Piggy bank almost doubled the money put in over 5 years. What does that mean for the future?
options: It's the past: the future may be different, even a loss
In 5 years, the money will definitely double
The Piggy bank never goes into the red
You should invest all your savings right away
quiz.why: Past results don't guarantee future ones. In that same test, there was a moment when the Piggy bank was worth 49% less than what had been put in.

lessons.title: Are drawdowns normal?
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know what a drawdown is and how not to panic when the price falls.

cards.title: The price moves like a roller coaster
cards.text: Crypto rarely rises smoothly. It shoots up, drops, and shoots up again, like a roller coaster. These big price swings are called volatility. The higher it is, the harder the price gets thrown up and down in a short time.
cards.example: In real life: spring weather. Sun in the morning, hail in the afternoon, warm again by evening. Changes are perfectly normal.

chart.caption: Illustrative example

cards.title: What a drawdown is
cards.text: A drawdown is how far the price has fallen from its peak. For example, a coin was worth $100 and is now $70. That's a 30% drawdown. Until you sell, you have the same number of coins. Only today's price has changed. It may come back — or it may not.
cards.example: In real life: an apartment was worth $50,000, but in a crisis buyers offer only $40,000. If you don't sell, you're still living in the same apartment.

cards.title: The trap: −50% and +100%
cards.text: If the price falls 50%, it needs to rise 100% to get back. Not 50%. It was $100, it halved — now it's $50. To get back to $100, you need $50 + 100% = $100. That's why big drops are so hard to win back.
cards.example: In real life: a shop cuts a price in half, from $100 to $50. To get back to $100, it has to raise the price by 100%.

chart.caption: Falling by half takes doubling to recover

cards.title: Even bitcoin has big drops
cards.text: Even bitcoin has fallen by half or more several times in the past. That's not rare — it's part of the journey. So tell yourself in advance: “My portfolio could drop by half.” If that thought scares you, you've put in too much.
cards.example: When we tested our Piggy bank over 5 years, there was a moment at −49% of what had been put in. By October 19, 2026, the result was about +91%. The past, not a promise.

cards.title: Only spare money
cards.text: How do you ride the roller coaster calmly? Invest only spare money — money you don't need for food, rent or medical care. Then a drop is unpleasant, but not frightening. You won't have to sell at the very bottom because you suddenly need cash.
cards.example: In real life: on a roller coaster, what matters most is a tightly fastened belt. Spare money is that belt.

cards.title: What to do when the price falls
cards.text: Don't make decisions in a panic. Don't check the price every 5 minutes. Remember why you bought and for how long. If you're saving regularly, during a drop the same money buys more coins. But only buy more according to your plan, and never with your last money.
cards.example: In real life: a plane shakes as it flies through clouds, but the pilot doesn't change course in a panic. He sticks to the flight plan.

remember: A drawdown is a fall from the peak. In crypto, it happens often.
After −50%, it takes +100% to get back.
Only invest spare money, so you never have to sell in a panic.

quiz.q: A coin fell from $100 to $50. How much does it need to rise to be worth $100 again?
options: By 50%
By 25%
quiz.why: $50 + 100% = $100. Falling by half can only be won back by doubling.

quiz.q: What is a drawdown?
options: An exchange fee for buying
How far the price has fallen from its peak
A price rise after a fall
A fee for storing coins
quiz.why: A drawdown shows how far the price has dropped from its highest point.

quiz.q: What money can you invest in crypto?
options: Next month's rent money
Money borrowed at a low interest rate
All your savings at once, to earn more
Spare money you won't need for years
quiz.why: If you might suddenly need the money, you'll have to sell cheap during a drop. Spare money can wait calmly.

lessons.title: How to read a chart: candles in plain words
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to look at a candlestick chart and understand what it shows.

cards.title: Why candles
cards.text: The price changes every second. If you drew every single change, you'd get a scribble. So the price is grouped into “candles.” Each candle sums up a slice of time: an hour, a day, a week.
cards.example: In real life: a thermometer changes every minute. But a forecast keeps it short: a high of 20° in the day, a low of 10° at night.

cards.title: Four numbers in one candle
cards.text: A candle holds 4 numbers: the price at the start of the period, the price at the end, the highest price and the lowest. The thick part of the candle — the body — runs from the start to the end. Thin wicks on the top and bottom reach the highest and lowest prices.
cards.example: Example: a one-day candle. In the morning $100, during the day up to $110, down to $95, in the evening $105. The body goes from $100 to $105, and the wicks reach $110 and $95.

cards.title: Green and red
cards.text: The color tells you where the price went. A green candle: the price ended higher than it started. A red one: it ended lower. The candle in our example is green, because $105 is more than $100. A long candle means the price moved a lot. A short one means it barely moved.
cards.example: In real life: a soccer match. The game had its ups and downs, but there's only one final score. A candle is that final score.

cards.title: Wicks tell a story
cards.text: A long wick at the bottom: the price was pushed down hard, but bounced back by the end. A long wick at the top: the price was pushed up, but couldn't stay there. Wicks are traces of the tug-of-war inside the period. But one candle promises nothing. Always look at many candles in a row.
cards.example: In real life: a child jumping on a trampoline. They fly up high but land in the same spot. The top wick is the height of the jump.

cards.title: A timeframe is like a map's zoom
cards.text: A timeframe is how much time one candle covers: 5 minutes, an hour, a day, a week. It's like zooming a map. Zoom out, and you see the whole country but not the streets. Zoom in, and you see the backyard but not the country. Same market, just a different view.
cards.example: Example: on 5-minute candles, the price jumps up and down. On weekly candles, you can see where it went all year.

cards.title: Less noise, more calm
cards.text: The smaller the timeframe, the more noise and nerves. A 5-minute candle can be red while the weekly candle is green. It's the same price, just a different zoom. If you're saving for years, daily and weekly candles are easier to follow.
cards.example: In real life: if you weigh yourself every hour, the numbers jump around. Once a week, you can see where you're really heading.

remember: A candle sums up a period: the start, the end, the highest and the lowest price.
Green means the price rose by the end; red means it fell.
A timeframe is a zoom level. For long-term investing, look at days and weeks.

quiz.q: A one-day candle: $100 in the morning, $90 in the evening. What color is it?
options: Green
Red
It depends on the highest price
Gray
quiz.why: The price ended lower than it started: $90 is less than $100. So the candle is red.

quiz.q: What do a candle's thin wicks show?
options: The price at the start and the end
How many people bought the coin
A forecast for tomorrow
The highest and lowest price during the period
quiz.why: The body runs from the start to the end. The wicks reach the highest and lowest prices during that time.

quiz.q: What is a timeframe?
options: How much time one candle covers
The exchange's opening hours
How long you've invested your money for
The time when news comes out
quiz.why: A timeframe is like a map's zoom: 1 candle can be 5 minutes, a day or a week.

lessons.title: Altcoins and meme coins: why they're riskier
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why small coins are riskier than bitcoin.

cards.title: What altcoins are
cards.text: An altcoin is any coin other than bitcoin. The name comes from “alternative coin.” Ether and solana are altcoins too, just big ones. And there are thousands of small ones. Some are building useful projects. Others run on nothing but hype and promises.
cards.example: In real life: besides the big chain stores, there are thousands of small shops. Some last for years; others close after a month.

cards.title: A big ship and small boats
cards.text: Bitcoin is like a big ship. It rocks in a storm too. A small coin is like a little boat: the same wave tosses it around much harder. A boat can shoot up to the crest of a wave fast. Or it can capsize just as fast. The smaller the coin, the bigger both the rises and the falls.
cards.example: Example: bitcoin moved 3% in a day. On that same day, a small coin might have moved 30% — up or down.

cards.title: Many coins disappear
cards.text: Over the years, thousands of coins have appeared in crypto. Many are now worth almost nothing: the team left, the project was abandoned, no one wants to buy anymore. It happens a lot. So a small coin isn't a “cheap bitcoin.” It's a separate and much bigger risk.
cards.example: In real life: a café opens with loud advertising, and six months later there's a different one in its place. Advertising doesn't make a business reliable.

cards.title: Meme coins are like lottery tickets
cards.text: Meme coins are made as a joke: with a dog, a cat or a funny picture. Usually there's no real business behind them, just the crowd's interest. The price can multiply in a week and then drop almost to zero. It's like a lottery ticket: once in a while you win, but usually you don't.
cards.example: In real life: people only spend money on lottery tickets that they don't mind losing. Same with meme coins.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: a meme coin's price over one week

cards.title: Why you only hear about the wins
cards.text: You hear stories like “I bought a tiny coin and got rich.” But the people who lost money rarely talk about it. Winners brag; losers stay quiet. So it seems like everyone's getting lucky. A loud story is no reason to buy.
cards.example: In real life: lottery wins make the news. Nobody writes about the losing tickets, even though there are far more of them.

cards.title: If you really want to
cards.text: If you really want small coins, keep them a small part — an amount you wouldn't mind losing completely. The core of your portfolio is major coins and a dollar reserve. Small coins are like salt in soup: a pinch is fine, a whole packet is not.
cards.example: In real life: you can't save an over-salted soup. That's why you add salt a little at a time and taste as you go.

remember: An altcoin is any coin other than bitcoin.
The smaller the coin, the bigger the rises and the falls.
A meme coin is like a lottery ticket: only money you don't mind losing.

quiz.q: What is an altcoin?
options: Only meme coins
A crypto dollar
Any coin other than bitcoin
A new version of bitcoin
quiz.why: “Alt” is short for “alternative.” Ether and solana are altcoins too, just big ones.

quiz.q: Why is a small coin riskier than bitcoin?
options: Its price gets thrown around harder, and the project might disappear
Because it costs less than $1
Because it can't be kept in a wallet
Because it's taxed
quiz.why: Like a little boat, a small coin gets tossed harder by the waves. And many such coins end up worth almost nothing over time.

quiz.q: A friend says he made 10 times his money on a meme coin. What's a sensible thought?
options: I need to buy the same coin right away
Meme coins always grow like that
So it must be a reliable coin
He got lucky; many people lose money on coins like that
quiz.why: You see the people who got lucky, while the losers stay quiet. A meme coin is like a lottery: you can lose everything.

lessons.title: Halving and bitcoin's cycles
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to explain what a halving is and why everyone talks about it.

cards.title: Where new bitcoins come from
cards.text: No one prints new bitcoins. They go to miners — owners of powerful computers that check and record every transfer on the network. About every 10 minutes, a new block appears: a page of records. For each one, the miner gets a reward in new coins.
cards.example: In real life: a bookkeeper keeps a shared ledger. They get paid for every page they fill. Only here, the pay is in fresh bitcoin.

cards.title: What a halving is
