cards.text: About every 4 years, the miners' reward is cut in half. That's the halving. It happened in 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. The next one is expected around April 2028. This rule has been built into bitcoin from the very start.
cards.example: In real life: a bakery that's allowed to bake less and less bread. Every 4 years, half as much as before.

chart.caption: Miner's reward per block, in bitcoin

cards.title: Fewer and fewer new coins
cards.text: After each halving, half as many new coins appear. From 2020 to 2024, it was about 900 a day. After the 2024 halving, it's about 450. And there will never be more than 21,000,000 bitcoins in total. The further along we go, the more slowly they're added.
cards.example: In real life: gold. The harder it is to mine, the more people value what already exists. But it's still people who set the price.

cards.title: What happened after halvings
cards.text: In the past, bitcoin's price rose sharply within a year to a year and a half after a halving. Then came big drops. That's where the idea of 4-year “cycles” comes from. But it's an observation, not a law of nature. That's how it went in the past — there are no guarantees.
cards.example: In real life: “a cold winter means a hot summer.” Sometimes it works out that way, but no one can promise the weather a year ahead.

cards.title: Why the cycles might break
cards.text: Today, lots of other things affect the price: big funds and companies, laws, world events. And everyone knows about a halving in advance, so many try to buy before it. That's why the old pattern may not repeat. Building your plan around halvings alone isn't a good idea.
cards.example: In real life: everyone knows about the Saturday sale. Lots of people come early, and by Saturday the best stuff is gone.

cards.title: What it means for your Piggy bank
cards.text: Good news: the Piggy bank doesn't need to guess the cycles. You buy a little before the halving and after it. When the price rises and when it falls. That way, your plan doesn't depend on whether the past repeats itself.
cards.example: In real life: you water your garden regularly, not only when the radio forecasts a heat wave.

remember: A halving: about every 4 years, the miners' reward is cut in half.
Halvings happened in 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. The next is around April 2028.
In the past, the price rose after halvings, but that's not a law.

quiz.q: What happens during a halving?
options: Bitcoin's price is cut in half
The miners' reward per block is cut in half
Everyone's coins are cut in half
Exchanges close for a day
quiz.why: Only the reward for a new block is cut in half. Your coins don't shrink because of it.

quiz.q: How often does a halving happen?
options: Every year
Every 10 minutes
About every 4 years
Whenever the exchanges decide
quiz.why: Halvings happened in 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024. The next one is expected around April 2028.

quiz.q: The price rose after past halvings. Does that mean it will happen again?
options: Yes, it's bitcoin's law
Yes, but only in 10 years
Yes, if everyone buys
No, it's an observation, with no guarantees
quiz.why: The past doesn't promise the future. Lots of things affect the price, and the pattern may not repeat.

lessons.title: How much to invest
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to estimate how much you can comfortably invest.

cards.title: First, a safety cushion
cards.text: Before you invest, build a safety cushion. That's enough to cover 3–6 months of everyday life: food, housing, transportation, medicine. Keep it separate, in regular money, not in crypto. It's there in case of illness, repairs or losing your job.
cards.example: In real life: the spare tire in your car. It doesn't move you forward. But without it, any nail on the road becomes a big problem.

cards.title: Working out your cushion
cards.text: Figure out how much you spend in a month. Multiply by 3 — that's the minimum. By 6 — that's more comfortable. Example: you spend $800 a month. Your cushion is from $800 × 3 = $2,400 to $800 × 6 = $4,800. Until you have it, save for that first, not for crypto.
cards.example: In real life: firewood for the winter is gathered in summer, not on the first frosty day.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: a cushion for $800 of monthly spending

cards.title: Only money for the long haul
cards.text: Only invest money you won't need for at least 2–3 years. Why so long? The price can fall by half and take a long time to come back. If you need the money in six months for a vacation or tuition, it may not be there when you need it.
cards.example: In real life: you don't plant an apple tree if you need apples by Friday. A tree takes years. Money for Friday stays in your wallet.

cards.title: Never with borrowed money
cards.text: Never invest a loan, a credit, or money borrowed from friends. If the price falls, the debt doesn't go anywhere. The bank doesn't care that your coins got cheaper. You'll have to pay out of your own pocket, plus interest. That's a double hit.
cards.example: Example: you borrowed $1,000, and your coins fell 50%. You have $500, but you owe the bank $1,000 plus interest.

cards.title: A simple order of steps
cards.text: Step 1: pay off expensive debts, like credit cards. Step 2: build a cushion for 3–6 months. Step 3: choose an amount you could live with even if it fell by half. Step 4: invest it a little at a time, regularly — for example, through the Piggy bank.
cards.example: In real life: you build a house from the foundation up, not from the roof. A solid base first, then everything else.

cards.title: The sleep test, and age
cards.text: A simple test: if the amount you have in crypto keeps you up at night, it's too much. Cut it down. And one important thing: you can only invest real money if you're 18 or older. Until then, learn on a demo account: real prices, virtual money.
cards.example: In real life: you can learn to drive on a closed practice lot. But you need a license to go out on the road.

remember: First a cushion for 3–6 months of spending, then investing.
Only invest money you won't need for 2–3 years.
Never invest borrowed money.

quiz.q: You spend $1,000 a month. What's the minimum safety cushion you need?
quiz.why: The minimum is 3 months of spending: $1,000 × 3 = $3,000. More comfortable is 6 months: $6,000.

quiz.q: You'll need some money in 4 months for home repairs. Should you invest it in crypto?
options: Yes, it might have time to grow
Yes, if you invest only half
Yes, if you buy only bitcoin
No: the price could drop a lot in 4 months
quiz.why: A short time frame means big risk. Only invest money you won't need for 2–3 years.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you invest money from a loan?
options: If prices fall, the debt stays while your money shrinks
It's against the law in every country
Loan money can't be transferred to an exchange
The bank will take the coins you bought
quiz.why: Coins can get cheaper, but a debt with interest doesn't. You'll have to repay it with your own money.

lessons.title: Keep a record of your purchases
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to keep a simple purchase log and see your real results honestly.

cards.title: Memory plays tricks on us
cards.text: After a year, few people remember when they bought and at what price. Memory loves the wins: “I got a great price here.” The bad buys get forgotten. So things seem better or worse than they really are. A simple habit helps: write it down.
cards.example: In real life: it feels like groceries don't cost that much. Then you add up a month of receipts — and get a surprise.

cards.title: What to write down
cards.text: A log is just a notebook or a spreadsheet. One line per purchase: the date, which coin, how much money you spent, at what price, and how many coins you got. If you sell, write that down too. Each entry takes a minute.
cards.example: Example line: Oct 12, 2026, bitcoin, $80 at a price of $80,000, received 0.001 bitcoin. Check: $80 ÷ $80,000 = 0.001.

cards.title: Your honest result
cards.text: Add up all the money you've put in. Look at what your coins are worth now. The difference is your real result. Not how it feels, but the actual numbers. This shows whether your plan is working.
cards.example: Example: 52 purchases of $50 over a year. Total put in: $50 × 52 = $2,600. The coins are now worth $2,900. Result: $2,900 − $2,600 = +$300.

cards.title: Your average price
cards.text: Your log will show your average purchase price. Divide all the money you put in by all the coins you got. If the price now is above your average, you're up. If it's below, you're down. One number instead of dozens of purchases.
cards.example: Example: $50 at a price of $10 gets you 5 coins. $25 at a price of $5 gets you 5 more. That's $75 for 10 coins: $75 ÷ 10 = $7.50 per coin.

cards.title: Taxes: check with a professional
cards.text: Crypto tax rules differ from country to country, and they change. Since 2026, exchanges in many countries collect data on their clients' trades for the tax authorities. We don't give tax advice. Find out the rules from a tax professional in your country. Your log will be a big help here: all the dates and amounts will be right at hand.
cards.example: In real life: it's best to see a doctor with your test results in hand. And to see a tax professional with your purchase log.

cards.title: Where to keep your log
cards.text: A notebook, notes on your phone or a spreadsheet all work. The exchange keeps a history too, but your own log is easier to follow. The key is to write things down right away, not “later.” Once a month, look at the total: how much you've put in and what it's worth now. Don't draw conclusions from a single day.
cards.example: In real life: a workout journal. You can't see progress in one day. But after six months, it's all there.

remember: Record every purchase: date, amount, price, how many coins.
Result = what it's worth now minus what you put in.
Taxes depend on your country — check with a professional.

quiz.q: What's important to record for every purchase?
options: Just the name of the coin
The news that made you buy
The date, amount, price and how many coins you got
The market mood that day
quiz.why: These 4 things let you honestly work out your result and your average price later.

quiz.q: You've put in $2,600, and your coins are now worth $2,400. What's your result?
quiz.why: $2,400 − $2,600 = −$200. A log tells you the truth, even when it's unpleasant.

quiz.q: How do you find out what tax to pay on crypto?
options: Check with a tax professional in your country
Crypto isn't taxed anywhere
The rules are the same everywhere
Ask other investors in a chat
quiz.why: Every country has its own rules, and they change. It's safer to ask a professional, and your purchase log will help them.

lessons.title: Cold wallet: step by step
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to set up a cold wallet safely and not lose coins through a setup mistake.

cards.title: What a cold wallet is
cards.text: A cold wallet is a small device that looks like a USB stick. The key to your coins lives inside it and never goes online. Even if your phone or computer catches a virus, stealing the key this way is much harder. “Cold” means “not connected to the internet”.
cards.example: In real life: an exchange is the cash in your pocket, and a cold wallet is the safe at home. You don't open the safe every day, but it's more secure.

cards.title: When you need one
cards.text: If the amount on the exchange is money you could afford to lose, you can skip the device. If losing it would really hurt, a cold wallet is worth it. It usually costs $60 to $200.
cards.example: Example: you hold $3 000 in bitcoin for years. A $100 device is about 3% of that: $100 ÷ $3 000 ≈ 3%.

cards.title: Buying it and the box
cards.text: Buy only from the maker's official website or its official partners — not second-hand and not on a random marketplace. Check that the seal on the box is intact. If there's already a card with printed words inside, it's a trap: don't use the device and send it back.
cards.example: In real life: you don't buy a front-door lock from a stranger who has already handed out its keys.

cards.title: Setup: PIN and 24 words
cards.text: When you first turn it on, choose a PIN — the device's code. Then the device itself shows 12 or 24 words — the seed phrase. Write them in order on paper or a metal plate and check twice. Don't photograph them or save them in notes, the cloud or a chat.
cards.example: Example: 24 words = 24 lines on a card. One wrong word and you can't restore the wallet from that record. That's why checking is a must.

cards.title: The first transfer is small
cards.text: First send a small amount from the exchange, for example $10. Check the receiving address on the device's own screen, not only on the computer: a virus can swap the address. If it arrives, everything is set up right and you can move the rest.
cards.example: Example: you sent $10 and $10 minus the network fee arrived. Only then — the main amount.

cards.title: A backup copy and scammers
cards.text: Keep the seed phrase record somewhere safe and a second copy in another place, in case of fire or flood. Scammers write as “support” and ask for the words “to verify”. Real support never asks: whoever knows the words owns the coins.
cards.example: In real life: you keep a spare flat key with your family, not under the doormat.

remember: Buy the device only from the official maker and check the seal.
The seed phrase lives only on paper or metal, never in a phone or the cloud.
First a small transfer, and check the address on the device's screen.

quiz.q: There's a card with 24 printed words in your new wallet's box. What do you do?
options: Use those words — it's faster
Photograph the card just in case
Don't use the device and return it to the seller
Copy the words into your phone's notes
quiz.why: An honest device creates the words itself during setup. Ready-made words in the box mean a fake: the scammer already knows your key.

quiz.q: Where should you keep the seed phrase?
options: In the cloud, so it doesn't get lost
On paper or metal in a safe place, plus a copy in another place
In a chat with support
In a screenshot on your phone
quiz.why: Anything online can be stolen. Paper or metal in two safe places protects you from both thieves and fire.

quiz.q: You're moving $2 000 to a new wallet. What's the right way?
options: Send it all at once
First $10, check it arrived, and only then the rest
To the address from a “support” email
Through a friend
quiz.why: A small transfer checks that the address and network are right. A mistake costs $10, not $2 000.

lessons.title: Digital inheritance: so your crypto isn't lost to your family
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to make a simple plan so your loved ones can find and receive your coins if something happens to you.

cards.title: Why crypto gets lost
cards.text: Heirs can find a bank deposit through documents. Crypto is different: if nobody knows where your coins are and how to reach them, they can be lost for good. So it's better to think about inheritance in advance — it takes 15 minutes and one sheet of paper.
cards.example: In real life: people write a will not because something will happen tomorrow, but to make things easier for the family later.

cards.title: A plan on one page
cards.text: Write down: which exchanges you have accounts on and which email they use, whether you have a cold wallet, the rough amount and who your heir is. No passwords and no seed phrases — only what is where. Keep the plan somewhere safe and tell someone close to you where to find it.
cards.example: Example plan: “Exchange: account on ivan@… · Cold wallet: in the safe at home · Words: in an envelope at the notary · Heir: my wife Anna”.

cards.title: Exchange accounts
cards.text: An exchange hands money to heirs only through its support team and with documents. Usually they ask for a death certificate, ID of the owner and the heir, and proof of the right to inherit. Each exchange has its own process, and it depends on your country's law. The key thing is that your family knows the account exists at all.
cards.example: Example: the heir submits a request to the exchange's support and uploads the documents. After the check, the coins go to the heir's account. The check can take weeks.

cards.title: Cold wallet
cards.text: There's no support here: the coins go to whoever has the seed phrase. So keep it where your family will find it but strangers won't: in a sealed envelope in a safe, a bank deposit box or with a notary — whatever is usual in your country.
cards.example: In real life: you don't leave the safe key on the table, but you don't hide it so well that nobody ever finds it either.

cards.title: Legacy Contact on iPhone
cards.text: On iPhone you can add a Legacy Contact: Settings → your name → Sign-In & Security → Legacy Contact. With the access key and a death certificate, they get your iCloud photos, notes, files and backups. They don't get Keychain passwords or money on exchanges. But if your plan is in iCloud Notes, your heir will find it.
cards.example: Example: you keep your plan in an iCloud note and made your son your Legacy Contact. He'll see what is where, but without passwords.

cards.title: What to remember
cards.text: CRYPTO NOVA never asks for or stores your passwords and seed phrases — and no honest service will ask. Update the plan once a year: a new account — add it. This is not legal advice: for inheritance in your country, talk to a notary or a lawyer.
cards.example: In real life: you check your insurance and documents once a year. Same with your inheritance plan.

remember: Your family must know where your coins are — from a one-page plan, without passwords.
An exchange pays heirs against documents; a cold wallet opens only with the seed phrase.
For inheritance law in your country — a notary or a lawyer.

quiz.q: What goes into an inheritance plan?
options: All passwords and seed phrases in one file
Which accounts and wallets are where and who the heir is — no passwords
Only the amount in the accounts
Nothing: the exchange will find the family
quiz.why: The plan shows what is where. Passwords in one file are a gift for a thief.

quiz.q: How does an heir get the money from an exchange account?
options: Only the email password is needed
Through the exchange's support — with documents on the death and the right to inherit
Through the iPhone Legacy Contact
There's no way, the money is gone
quiz.why: An exchange hands coins to heirs after checking documents. Each exchange has its own process.

quiz.q: What does an iPhone Legacy Contact give?
options: Access to the money on an exchange
Keychain passwords
iCloud photos, notes and files — for example, your inheritance plan
Nothing
quiz.why: A Legacy Contact gets iCloud data, but not passwords or money on exchanges. That's why a plan in iCloud Notes is a handy hint for your family.

lessons.title: Compound growth: why time matters more than the sum
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will see why starting early often matters more than a big sum.

cards.title: Interest on interest
cards.text: Income that stays invested earns income too. That is compound growth. $1,000 at +10% a year becomes $1,100 after a year and $1,210 after two — not $1,200.
cards.example: In real life: a snowball — the longer it rolls, the faster it grows.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: $1,000 at a steady +10% a year, $

cards.title: Time beats the sum
cards.text: The earlier you start, the longer growth works for you. At 7% a year, $10,000 becomes about $19,700 in 10 years and about $76,000 in 30 years. Same money — the only difference is time.
cards.example: In real life: a tree planted 20 years earlier gives shade that money cannot buy.

cards.title: The rule of 72
cards.text: A quick mental check: 72 ÷ the yearly percentage ≈ how many years it takes to double. At 8% a year — about 9 years, at 6% — 12.
cards.example: In real life: the «about an hour per 60 km» estimate — not exact, but instantly clear.

cards.title: But growth is not smooth
cards.text: In real life returns do not arrive evenly every year. Bitcoin has had years of −60% and +150%. Compounding works over the long run if you do not sell everything in a panic during a drawdown. Growth is not guaranteed.
cards.example: In real life: a mountain road — ups and downs, and only at the end do you see how high you climbed.

remember: Income on income speeds up growth over time.
Rule of 72: 72 ÷ % a year ≈ years to double.
Real growth is uneven and not guaranteed.

quiz.q: $1,000 at +10% a year. How much after 2 years with compounding?
quiz.why: $1,000 × 1.1 = $1,100, then $1,100 × 1.1 = $1,210. The second year also added interest on the first year's income.

quiz.q: By the rule of 72: in how many years does money double at 6% a year?
What hurts compounding most?
options: A long time frame
Selling everything in a panic during a drawdown
Regular top-ups
Patience
quiz.why: Selling in a drawdown cuts the growth short and locks in the loss. Compounding needs time.

lessons.title: Rebalancing: keeping your shares in order
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will be able to bring your portfolio back to its planned shares and see why it matters.

cards.title: Shares drift on their own
cards.text: You decided to hold 60% in bitcoin and 40% in dollars: $6,000 and $4,000. Bitcoin doubled — now it is $12,000 and $4,000, that is 75% and 25%. The risk grew by itself, without your decision.
cards.example: In real life: a garden bed left unweeded — the weeds crowd out everything else.

chart.caption: The plan was 60/40 — after bitcoin's rise it is 75/25

cards.title: Put it back
cards.text: Rebalancing means selling part of what grew and buying more of what lagged. The total is $16,000; the 60/40 target is $9,600 and $6,400. Sell bitcoin worth $12,000 − $9,600 = $2,400.
cards.example: In real life: trimming the bushes so one does not block the sun for the rest.

cards.title: When to do it
cards.text: Usually on a schedule — say once a quarter — or when a share has drifted far, for example by 10 percentage points. Too often means extra fees; too rarely lets the risk grow.
cards.example: In real life: a car gets its service on schedule, not every day.

cards.title: Why bother
cards.text: Rebalancing makes you sell a little of what got expensive and buy what got cheap — without emotions. It does not promise higher returns, but it keeps the risk at the level you chose.
cards.example: In real life: a rule like «no more than two desserts» works better than deciding anew each time.

remember: One coin's growth changes the shares and the risk.
Rebalancing brings back the planned shares.
Do it on a schedule or when the drift is large.

quiz.q: Plan 50/50. Now $15,000 in bitcoin and $5,000 in dollars. How much bitcoin to sell to get back to 50/50?
quiz.why: The total is $20,000, half is $10,000. Sell $15,000 − $10,000 = $5,000 and bring dollars up to $10,000.

quiz.q: Why rebalance?
options: It guarantees profit
It keeps the risk at the chosen level
It cancels taxes
It cancels drawdowns
quiz.why: The main job is to stop one coin from quietly becoming almost the whole portfolio.

quiz.q: What is wrong with rebalancing every day?
options: Extra fees
It is forbidden
The exchange will block the account
Nothing
quiz.why: Every trade costs money. Small daily adjustments eat the returns.

lessons.title: A safety cushion: before you invest
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will know how much money to set aside before your first investment.

cards.title: The cushion comes first
cards.text: A safety cushion is money for 3–6 months of usual spending. It sits separately, is available at once and is not put into risky assets.
cards.example: In real life: the spare wheel in the boot. You do not need it while all is well, but nobody drives without it.

cards.title: Why an investor needs it
cards.text: Without a cushion any surprise — a repair, an illness, a lost job — forces you to sell your investments. Often right in a drawdown, at a loss.
cards.example: In real life: selling the harvest green because you suddenly need cash.

cards.title: How much and where
cards.text: Take a month's spending and multiply by 3–6. If you spend $800 a month, the cushion is $2,400–4,800. Keep it somewhere safe with quick access: a deposit or an account you can withdraw from within a day.
cards.example: In real life: the first-aid kit is kept at home, not at the country house.

chart.caption: A cushion for $800 of monthly spending, $

cards.title: Then — the piggy bank
cards.text: Once the cushion is in place, invest only spare money — money you will not need for several years. You can start with a small sum once a week.
cards.example: In real life: first a roof over your head, then the garden.

remember: A cushion is 3–6 months of spending, kept separate and at hand.
Without it, a surprise forces you to sell in a drawdown.
Invest only spare money.

quiz.q: You spend $1,000 a month. What is a 3–6 month cushion?
Where should the cushion be kept?
options: In meme coins
In leveraged futures
Somewhere safe with quick access
It does not need to be kept
quiz.why: The cushion must stay whole and available on any day. Risky assets do not suit it.

quiz.q: Why is investing without a cushion dangerous?
options: Unexpected costs force you to sell, perhaps at a loss
The exchange will not open an account
Fees will be lower
Nothing will happen
quiz.why: The money will be needed at the worst moment — and you will have to sell at any price.

lessons.title: Exchange-traded funds (ETFs): crypto through a broker
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand what a crypto ETF is and how it differs from buying coins on an exchange.

cards.title: What an ETF is
cards.text: An ETF is a fund whose shares you buy on a stock exchange, just like a stock. A crypto ETF holds real coins. The fund keeps the coins, and you hold a share of the fund in your brokerage account.
cards.example: In real life: instead of keeping a gold bar at home, you buy a share in a vault. The bar stays there, and you hold a certificate for your share.

cards.title: Which funds exist
cards.text: In the US, bitcoin funds have traded since January 2024 and ether funds since July 2024. Since autumn 2025, funds for solana, XRP and other coins have appeared: the regulator simplified the rules for launching them. In Europe, similar exchange-traded products are called ETPs. As of October 2026, both individuals and big companies hold bitcoin through such funds.
cards.example: Example: the largest bitcoin fund charges about 0.25% a year. On $1,000, that's $2.50 a year.

cards.title: Pros and cons
cards.text: Pros: you buy through a familiar broker, you don't need to keep keys, and a regulator watches the fund. Cons: trading only during stock exchange hours, a fee to the fund every year, and you can't withdraw the coins themselves to your own wallet. The price swings just like the coin's.
cards.example: In real life: an ETF is like a taxi, and your own coin is like your own car. In a taxi you don't think about repairs, but you ride by its rules and pay for the trip.

cards.title: Which to choose
cards.text: If you just want to hold bitcoin for years in a brokerage account, an ETF is convenient. If you want to save a little at a time, move coins and use crypto services, you need the coins themselves on an exchange or in a wallet. Which funds are available depends on your country. The risk is the same: a fall in bitcoin hits the fund too.
cards.example: In real life: tea comes in bags or loose. It's the same tea, but convenience and price differ.

remember: An ETF is a share in a fund that holds real coins.
Convenient through a broker, but there's a fund fee and you can't withdraw the coins.
The fund's price swings with the coin: the risk is the same.

quiz.q: What do you buy when you buy a bitcoin ETF?
options: A share of a fund that holds bitcoins
The bitcoins themselves, to your own wallet
A share in the BingX exchange
Protection from a price fall
quiz.why: The fund keeps the coins, and you hold a share in your brokerage account. An ETF doesn't protect you from a price fall.

quiz.q: Since when have bitcoin funds traded in the US?
options: Since 2009
Since January 2024
Since 2030
They don't exist
quiz.why: The first bitcoin ETFs started trading in the US in January 2024, and ether ETFs in July 2024.

quiz.q: A fund charges 0.25% a year. How much is that on $2,000?
quiz.why: $2,000 × 0.25% = $5 a year. Not much, but the fee is charged every year you hold the fund.

lessons.title: Taxes and exchange reports: what changed in 2026
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know what data exchanges pass to tax authorities and how to prepare for it.

cards.title: Exchanges started reporting
cards.text: Since 1 January 2026, under new rules — DAC8 in the EU and CARF worldwide — exchanges in 48 countries, including the EU and the UK, collect data on their clients' trades. From 2027, this data will start going to tax authorities. Dozens more countries will join later. This is as of October 2026.
cards.example: In real life: the tax office already knows your salary from your employer. Now the exchange reports your trades too.

cards.title: In the US: Form 1099-DA
cards.text: In the US, exchanges send clients Form 1099-DA. For 2025 trades it shows only the sale amounts. For 2026 trades it also shows the purchase price. You still work out the profit and the tax yourself.
cards.example: Example: you sold bitcoin for $1,000 that you bought for $800. The exchange reports the $1,000, and you work out and declare the $200 difference yourself.

cards.title: What tax is usually paid on
cards.text: In many countries, tax is paid on the profit when you sell coins or swap one coin for another. Profit is the difference between the sale price and the purchase price. Buying and simply holding usually don't create tax. But rates, rules and allowances differ in every country, and they change.
cards.example: Example: you bought coins for $500 and sold them for $650. The profit is $150. That's what tax is calculated on, if your country has it.

cards.title: How to prepare
cards.text: Keep a log of your buys and sales — see the lesson “Keep a record of your purchases”. Save your exchange statements once a year. Check your country's rules with a tax professional. We don't give tax advice.
cards.example: In real life: people keep receipts for repairs so they don't have to argue about the warranty later. Exchange statements are the same kind of receipt.

remember: Since 2026, exchanges in many countries collect trade data for tax authorities.
Tax is usually paid on the profit when you sell or swap.
Keep a log and check the rules with a tax professional.

quiz.q: What changed on 1 January 2026?
options: Crypto was banned
Exchanges in the EU, the UK and other countries collect trade data for tax authorities
Crypto taxes were abolished
Exchanges stopped checking identity
quiz.why: Under DAC8 and CARF, exchanges collect data from 2026 and pass it to tax authorities from 2027.

quiz.q: You bought coins for $500 and sold them for $650. What amount is tax usually calculated on?
quiz.why: Tax is usually calculated on the profit: $650 − $500 = $150. The rate and rules depend on the country.

quiz.q: What helps you work out your tax calmly?
options: Deleting your trade history
A log of buys and sales plus exchange statements
Advice from a chat
Nothing: the exchange will calculate everything
quiz.why: To work out the profit you need the dates and prices of your buys. The exchange doesn't report everything — often you have to do the maths yourself.

lessons.title: Crypto laws: what changed by 2026
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know the main new rules for crypto and how to check that a service operates legally.

cards.title: There are more rules now
cards.text: Not long ago, crypto had almost no laws of its own. By 2026, major countries had passed them. The goal is for services to hold client money honestly, check who opens an account, and be honest about the risks. But every country has its own rules.
cards.example: In real life: when the roads filled with cars, driving licences, traffic lights and vehicle inspections appeared.

cards.title: Europe: the MiCA rules
cards.text: The MiCA rules apply in the EU. The transition period ended on 1 July 2026: now only companies with an EU licence may provide crypto services to EU residents. You can check a company in the register of the European regulator ESMA. Exchanges with an EU licence don't sell stablecoins that lack authorization, such as USDT.
cards.example: Example: you live in Spain. Before opening an account, look the exchange up in the ESMA register. If it isn't there, that's a reason to be careful.

cards.title: The US: the stablecoin law
cards.text: In July 2025, the US passed the GENIUS Act on stablecoins. Only vetted companies will be able to issue them, and the reserve must be held 1:1 in dollars and short-term US Treasury bills. A report on the reserve comes out every month. The law takes full effect by January 2027 at the latest.
cards.example: In real life: a bank must keep reserves. Now stablecoin issuers must also keep a reserve and show it.

cards.title: What it means for you
cards.text: Only use services that are allowed in your country, and don't get around bans: you lose the protection of the law, and your account can be closed. Laws don't protect you from a price fall — market risk stays yours. That's why CRYPTO NOVA names only an exchange that works in your country: in the EU it is OKX Europe, licensed under MiCA.
cards.example: In real life: car insurance doesn't save you from black ice. It helps if someone else is at fault, but you still need to drive carefully.

remember: By 2026, the EU and the US had laws for crypto.
In the EU, since 1 July 2026, crypto services require an EU licence.
Laws protect you from dishonest services, but not from a price fall.

quiz.q: You live in the EU. How do you check that an exchange operates legally?
options: By how nice its website looks
By reviews in a chat
Find it in the ESMA register
Ask a bot in a messenger app
quiz.why: Since 1 July 2026, only licensed companies provide crypto services in the EU. They're listed in the ESMA register.

quiz.q: What does the US GENIUS Act require?
options: That bitcoin costs $1
That a stablecoin has a 1:1 reserve in dollars and short-term US Treasury bills
That the government issues all coins
That exchanges charge no fees
quiz.why: The stablecoin law requires a full reserve and monthly reports on it.

quiz.q: Do the new laws protect you from a fall in the bitcoin price?
options: Yes, now the price can't fall
Yes, the government will cover losses
No: laws keep services honest, but market risk is yours
Only in the EU
quiz.why: Laws require honesty from exchanges and stablecoin issuers. But the price can still fall.

levels.level_sub: How a trade works: direction, leverage, stop, target and size

lessons.title: Spot vs. futures: what's the difference
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to explain how buying a coin differs from a futures trade.

cards.title: Spot: you buy it, it's yours
cards.text: Spot is an ordinary purchase. You pay money and get a coin. It sits in your account, like apples in your basket. If it gets more expensive, you're up. If it gets cheaper, you're down, but the coin is still yours.
cards.example: In real life: you buy 2 kg of apples at the market for $1 a kilo. Now they're yours. You can eat them, give them away or sell them later — for more or for less.

cards.title: Futures: a deal on the price
cards.text: A futures contract isn't the coin itself — it's a deal on its price. You don't receive or hold the coin. You make or lose money depending on where the price goes. Only the change in price matters.
cards.example: In real life: two neighbors agree on a price for potatoes this fall. No potatoes change hands. If the price goes up or down, one pays the other the difference.

cards.title: You can profit from a fall, too
cards.text: With spot, you only make money when the price goes up. With futures, you can pick a side: up or down. Guess the direction right — you're up. Guess wrong — you're down.
cards.example: In real life: two friends argue about the weekend weather. One expects sun, the other rain. With futures, you can take either side.

cards.title: Why the risk is higher
cards.text: Futures come with leverage — money the exchange lends you. It multiplies both profits and losses. If the price moves far enough against you, the exchange closes the trade itself, and the money you put into it is gone. With spot, you keep the coin even if it gets cheaper.
cards.example: In real life: a house bought with your own money stays yours, even in hard times. A house bought on credit can be taken by the bank if you stop paying.

cards.title: Calmer and bolder
cards.text: Spot is simpler: the coin is yours, and the trade won't close on its own. Futures suit people who understand the risk and always set a stop. CRYPTO NOVA has both: “Spot” with no leverage, and “Futures,” where every trade has a stop set in advance. Real money is for 18+ only.
cards.example: You can try it with no risk on a demo account: virtual money, real prices.

remember: Spot: you buy a coin, and it's yours.
Futures: a deal on the price — you can profit from both rises and falls.
Futures are riskier: because of leverage, a trade can be closed at a loss.

quiz.q: You bought bitcoin on spot, and the price fell 20%. What happens to your coin?
options: The exchange sells it right away
It disappears from your account
It's still yours; it's just worth less
It gets swapped for a futures contract
quiz.why: With spot, the coin is yours. The price can fall and rise, but no one takes the coin away or sells it on their own.

quiz.q: How do futures differ from spot?
options: A futures contract is a deal on the price; you don't hold the coin itself
A futures contract is a more expensive coin
Futures can only bet on a rise
Futures only trade at night
quiz.why: A futures contract is a deal on the price. You make or lose money as the price changes, but you don't get the coin itself.

quiz.q: Why is futures trading riskier than spot?
options: Different coins are sold there
The prices there aren't real
The risk is the same as with spot
Leverage makes losses bigger, and the trade can be closed
quiz.why: Leverage is borrowed money. It makes both profits and losses bigger. If the price moves hard against you, the exchange closes the trade.

lessons.title: Long and short
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand how you can make money from both rising and falling prices.

cards.title: Long: a bet on a rise
cards.text: A long is a trade on the price going up. You go in because you expect the price to rise. Buy cheaper, sell higher. The difference is your profit. If the price falls, the difference becomes a loss.
cards.example: In real life: you buy a bike in spring for $100 and sell it in summer for $120. You made $120 − $100 = $20. That's a long.

cards.title: Short: a bet on a fall
cards.text: A short is a trade on the price going down. Here, you make money if the price drops. Sounds odd: how can you profit from something getting cheaper? The secret is the order of steps. First sell high, then buy back lower.
cards.example: Usually, you buy and then sell. With a short, it's the other way around: you sell, then buy. The profit is the same price difference, just in reverse order.

cards.title: The neighbor's book
cards.text: Say a neighbor lends you a book for a week. Today, that book costs $20, and you sell it. A week later, the price has dropped to $15. You buy the same book and give it back to your neighbor. You've got $20 − $15 = $5 left in your pocket.
cards.example: On an exchange, it's even simpler: you don't have to borrow a coin by hand. A short opens with one button, and the exchange does the rest.

cards.title: If the price goes the wrong way
cards.text: With a short, a rising price is the danger. Say the book's price goes up to $30. You still have to give it back to your neighbor. You buy it for $30, but you sold it for $20. That's a loss of $30 − $20 = $10. That's why you decide on your exit in advance, in case you're wrong.
cards.example: With a long, it's the opposite: a falling price is the danger. Any direction can fail, and that's normal.

cards.title: What it looks like in the app
cards.text: CRYPTO NOVA trades show the direction plainly: “UP (LONG)” or “DOWN (SHORT)”. LONG means the system expects the price to rise. SHORT means it expects it to fall. It's a calculated bet, not a promise: the price can go the other way.
cards.example: In real life: a forecast of “rain tomorrow” doesn't promise rain. It says rain is more likely. A system trade is the same kind of forecast.

remember: Long: profit from a rise — buy lower, sell higher.
Short: profit from a fall — sell higher, buy back lower.
Any direction can turn out wrong, so the exit is planned in advance.

quiz.q: You think a coin's price will fall. What kind of trade do you open?
options: Long
Short
A spot purchase
A Piggy bank
quiz.why: A short is a trade on a fall. First you sell higher, then you buy back lower. The difference is your profit.

quiz.q: You opened a short at $20, and the price rose to $30. What's the result?
options: A $10 profit
A $30 profit
Nothing has changed
A $10 loss
quiz.why: With a short, a rising price means a loss. You sold at $20 but have to buy back at $30: $30 − $20 = $10 in the red.

quiz.q: What does LONG mean in a CRYPTO NOVA trade?
options: The system expects the price to rise
The trade is for the long haul, many years
The system expects the price to fall
Profit is guaranteed
quiz.why: LONG is a trade on the price going up. Despite the word, it has nothing to do with how long the trade lasts. And it's a forecast, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Leverage and liquidation
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand what leverage is and why it can wipe out a trade.

cards.title: Leverage is like a loan from the exchange
cards.text: Leverage is money the exchange lends you for a trade. Example: you have $100, and the exchange adds $900. Now the trade is worth $1,000. That's ×10 leverage: $100 × 10 = $1,000.
cards.example: In real life: a mortgage. You pay part of the apartment's price, and the bank provides the rest. The apartment is big, but the debt is yours.

cards.title: Profit multiplies
cards.text: The price rises 10%. The $1,000 trade is now $1,100. That's +$100, and only $100 of it was your money. So on your own money, you made +100%. That's why leverage is so tempting.
cards.example: Without leverage, the same $100 with a 10% rise would have made $10. ×10 leverage multiplied the result by 10.

cards.title: Losses multiply just the same
cards.text: Now the price falls 10%. The $1,000 trade is now $900. That's −$100 — all of your money. The $900 owed to the exchange is still there, but your part is gone. The exchange closes the trade itself. This is called liquidation.
cards.example: In real life: a boat costs $1,000: $100 is yours, and a friend lent you $900. The boat's value drops to $900 — your share is gone, and your friend takes the boat.

cards.title: The bigger the leverage, the closer the cliff
cards.text: Roughly: with ×10 leverage, a drop of about 10% closes the trade. With ×5, about 20%. With ×2, about 50%. Because of fees and exchange rules, it happens a bit sooner. Shorts work the same way, only a rising price is the danger. The exchange shows the exact liquidation price in the trade.
cards.example: In real life: the higher you stand on a ladder, the more dangerous a slip. Big leverage is a high rung.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: price drop until liquidation, %

cards.title: How to handle leverage
cards.text: Leverage is like a sharp knife: useful if you're careful. Small leverage, a stop every time, a small trade size. The stop closes the trade before liquidation, with a small loss. In CRYPTO NOVA trades, leverage is shown in the “Risk” block, for example “leverage ×2”.
cards.example: In real life: a kitchen knife is for slicing bread, not for waving around. Leverage only works for you when you handle it with care.

remember: Leverage is money the exchange lends you: profits and losses both multiply.
At ×10, a drop of about 10% wipes out your part. That's liquidation.
Your stop must come before the liquidation price.

quiz.q: You have $100 and ×10 leverage. How big is the trade?
quiz.why: Leverage multiplies the amount: $100 × 10 = $1,000. Of that, $100 is yours, and $900 is borrowed from the exchange.

quiz.q: A $1,000 trade with ×10 leverage, $100 of it your money. The price falls 10%. What happens?
options: You lose $10
Your $100 runs out, and the exchange closes the trade
Nothing, you just need to wait
The exchange lends you more money
quiz.why: $1,000 − 10% = $900. That's −$100 — all of your money. The exchange closes the trade: that's liquidation.

quiz.q: At which leverage can the price move furthest against you before liquidation?
quiz.why: The smaller the leverage, the further away liquidation is. At ×2, it takes a drop of about 50%; at ×10, about 10%.

lessons.title: Stop-loss: your seatbelt
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why every trade needs a stop and where to place it.

cards.title: Decide your exit in advance
cards.text: Before entering a trade, you decide: if the price reaches this point, I'm out. The loss will be small and known in advance. This kind of exit is called a stop-loss, or just a stop. The name says it all: it stops the loss.
cards.example: In real life: before going to the market, you decide: I won't spend more than $50. You set the limit at home, before your eyes start wandering.

cards.title: A seatbelt
cards.text: A stop is like a seatbelt in a car. You don't buckle up because you expect a crash. You do it so that if something goes wrong, the blow is softer. A trade without a stop is like driving without a seatbelt. Usually it's fine. But one day it might not be.
cards.example: In real life: no one buckles up in the middle of a crash. A stop, too, is set before you start, not when the price is already plunging.

cards.title: How a stop works
cards.text: A stop is an order to the exchange. You set a price, and the exchange closes the trade by itself when the price reaches it. Even if you're asleep or on the road. If the price moves very sharply, the stop may fill at a slightly worse price than the one you set.
cards.example: Example: you bought at $100 with a stop at $95. Then the price dropped to $85. The stop closed the trade at −5%, not −15%.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: entry $100, stop $95

cards.title: Where to put your stop
cards.text: A stop goes where your idea stops working. Example: you expected the price not to fall below $95, but it did. That means you were wrong, and it's time to get out. A stop isn't placed at random. And most importantly: you don't move it when the price gets close.
cards.example: In real life: you agreed to wait for a friend until 7 p.m. He doesn't show — you leave, rather than standing on the street until midnight.

cards.title: A small loss is normal
cards.text: A stop getting hit isn't a failure. It's the price of trying, like a ticket to a movie you didn't enjoy. The danger isn't small losses — it's one huge one. And a stop is exactly what keeps a small loss from becoming huge.
cards.example: Example: 5 losses of 2% each come to about −10%. One loss without a stop could be −50%. And after −50%, you need +100% just to get back.

remember: A stop is an exit price, set in advance, with a small loss.
Set the stop before you enter, and don't move it when the price gets close.
A trade without a stop is like driving without a seatbelt.

quiz.q: When is the right time to set a stop?
options: When the price has already dropped a lot
Only if the trade is in profit
A week after entering
Right when you open the trade
quiz.why: Like a seatbelt, a stop is set before the journey starts. When the price is already plunging, deciding is harder, and the loss is bigger.

quiz.q: You bought at $100 with a stop at $95. Then the price fell to $85. What's your loss?
options: About −5%
quiz.why: The stop closed the trade at around $95: $100 − $95 = $5, which is −5%. Without a stop, it would have been −15%.

quiz.q: The price is getting close to your stop. What do the rules say to do?
options: Move the stop further away — it might turn around
Leave the stop where it is
Remove the stop altogether
Buy more while it's cheap
quiz.why: The stop was decided in advance, with a calm head. If you keep moving it, a small loss can turn into a big one.

lessons.title: Targets and taking profit
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll know where to take your profit and why greed gets in the way.

cards.title: The target: where you take profit
cards.text: The target is also decided in advance: what price you're waiting for. When the price gets there, the trade closes, and the profit is in your account. This kind of exit in profit is called a take-profit. The name says it all: you take the profit.
cards.example: In real life: you're selling your apple harvest and decided in advance: I'll sell at $2 a kilo. A buyer comes along offering that price — you sell.

cards.title: Profit on screen isn't profit yet
cards.text: While a trade is open, the gain can vanish. The price gets almost to the target and turns around — and the gain melts to zero or turns into a loss. The profit is only yours once the trade is closed.
cards.example: Example: you bought at $100 with a target of $120. The target was hit: +20%. A day later, the price is already $109. Without a target, the gain could have melted away.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: entry $100, target $120

cards.title: Greed gets in the way
cards.text: The price hits your target, and you want to wait a bit longer. “What if it doubles?” That's greed talking. Sometimes the price really does keep rising, but often it turns around. A plan made in advance protects you from thoughts like these.
cards.example: In real life: you're selling your country cottage. A buyer offers a good price, but you hold out for more. The buyer walks away, and no one else turns up for six months.

cards.title: Taking partial profit
cards.text: There's a middle path. You close part of the trade at the first target and leave the rest for a second one. Some money is already in your pocket, and there's still a chance of a bigger rise. Sometimes the stop is then moved to the entry price, so the rest is almost risk-free.
cards.example: Example: you bought 10 coins at $5. At $6, you sold 5 coins: 5 × $1 = $5 profit. The other 5 coins wait for the $7 target.

cards.title: Target further than the stop
cards.text: A good trade usually stands to gain more than it risks. Example: stop at −5%, target at +10%. One winning trade covers two losing ones: 2 × 5% = 10%. In the app, you can see this in the “Risk” block as “reward / risk,” for example 3 : 1.
cards.example: In real life: a fisherman sets up 3 rods. Only one gets a bite, but it's a big fish — and the catch makes the whole day worth it.

remember: The target is decided in advance, just like the stop.
The profit is only yours once the trade is closed.
You can close part of a trade at the first target and leave the rest.

quiz.q: The price has reached your target. What does your plan say?
options: Wait until it doubles
Buy more with all your money
Close the trade, or part of it, as you decided
Remove the stop
quiz.why: You set the target with a calm head. The price got there — your plan says take the profit. Waiting beyond the plan is greed.

quiz.q: A trade is up +15%, but it's still open. Is that your profit already?
options: Yes, it's already in your account
Not yet: the price could turn around
Yes, if the trade has been open for more than a day
Yes, if it's bitcoin
quiz.why: While a trade is open, the gain can vanish. The profit becomes yours once the trade is closed.

quiz.q: You bought 10 coins at $5. At $6, you sold 5 coins. How much have you made so far?
quiz.why: Each coin made $6 − $5 = $1. You sold 5 coins: 5 × $1 = $5. The other 5 are waiting for their target.

lessons.title: Trade size: risk 1–2% of your account
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to size a trade so that one loss doesn't hurt your account.

cards.title: How much are you willing to lose
cards.text: Experienced traders don't start by asking “how much will I make?” They ask “how much am I willing to lose?” A common rule: risk 1–2% of your account on one trade. That's not the trade size. It's the amount you'll lose if the stop is hit.
cards.example: Example: you have $1,000 in your account. 1% is $10, and 2% is $20. That's how much you can lose on one trade, and no more.

cards.title: 5 losses in a row is no disaster
cards.text: Everyone has losing streaks. Example: you risk $10 per trade and hit 5 stops in a row. 5 × $10 = $50. You still have $950 of your $1,000. It's unpleasant, but you can calmly carry on.
cards.example: In real life: a soccer team loses 5 games in a row. If the squad is still intact, the season isn't lost yet.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: the account after 5 losses of $10

cards.title: What if you risk a lot
cards.text: Another example: you risk $200 per trade, which is 20% of your account. The same 5 stops in a row: 5 × $200 = $1,000. The account is gone. The bad week is exactly the same, but the outcome is completely different. Size made all the difference.
cards.example: Important: after losing half your account, you need +100% to get back. $500 has to double to become $1,000 again.

cards.title: How to work out your trade size
cards.text: You need 2 numbers: how much you're willing to lose, and how far the stop is from your entry. Divide the first by the second. Example: you're willing to lose $10, and the stop is 5% below the entry. $10 ÷ 5% = $200. A $200 trade: if the stop is hit, you'll be down about $10.
cards.example: Check: 5% of $200 = $10. A closer stop means the trade can be bigger. A further stop means a smaller trade.

cards.title: Risk in CRYPTO NOVA trades
cards.text: Every system trade has a “Risk” block that shows how much money is at risk. For example: “$50 of $10,000 at risk.” That's 0.5% of the account: what the demo account will lose if the stop is hit. If you repeat the trade, work out the risk from your own amount.
cards.example: Example: your account is $1,000, and the risk is 0.5% — that's $1,000 × 0.5% = $5 per trade.

remember: Risk 1–2% of your account per trade: on $1,000, that's $10–20.
Trade size = how much you're willing to lose ÷ distance to the stop.
With a small risk, 5 losses in a row aren't a catastrophe.

quiz.q: Your account holds $2,000. How much is a 1% risk per trade?
quiz.why: 1% of $2,000 = $2,000 ÷ 100 = $20. That's how much you'll lose if the stop is hit.

quiz.q: You're willing to lose $10, and the stop is 5% below the entry. How big should the trade be?
quiz.why: $10 ÷ 5% = $200. Check: 5% of $200 = $10. If the stop is hit, you'll be down about $10.

quiz.q: A $1,000 account, $200 risked per trade. You hit 5 stops in a row. What's left?
options: $0 — the account is gone
quiz.why: 5 × $200 = $1,000. The whole account went in one losing streak. With $10 risked per trade, you'd still have $950.

lessons.title: Funding in plain words
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why, on an open futures trade, sometimes you pay and sometimes you get paid.

cards.title: Traders paying each other
cards.text: On crypto exchanges, futures usually have no expiry: a trade has no end date. They come with a special fee. Traders betting on a rise (longs) and traders betting on a fall (shorts) pay each other, usually every few hours. This is called funding. This fee doesn't go to the exchange or to the app.
cards.example: In real life: neighbors share a boat. Whoever needs it more right now pays the other a bit extra for using it.

cards.title: Like paying for a place in line
cards.text: Picture a line for a hot new gadget. When everyone wants to join it, a spot in the line gets more expensive. Futures work the same way. When almost everyone is long, longs pay shorts. When almost everyone is short, shorts pay longs.
cards.example: In real life: in summer, everyone wants to rent a house by the sea, and rents go up. In winter, few people want one, and they pay less.

cards.title: Why it exists
cards.text: A futures contract has its own price. It can drift away from the price of the coin itself. Funding pulls it back. If the futures price is higher than the coin's, holding a long starts to cost money. Some longs close, and the prices come back together.
cards.example: In real life: a rubber band. Stretch it, and it pulls back. Funding works the same way, pulling the futures price back toward the coin's regular price.

cards.title: How much it is in money
cards.text: Funding is usually a fraction of a percent of the trade size. Example: a $1,000 trade with 0.01% funding. That's $1,000 × 0.01% = 10 cents per payment. Only traders with a trade open at the moment of payment pay or receive it.
cards.example: Example: 3 payments a day. Per day, that's 3 × 10 cents = 30 cents. Per month, about 30 × 30 cents = $9.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: funding on a $1,000 trade, in dollars

cards.title: What it means for you
cards.text: For a quick trade, funding is barely noticeable. For a long one, it adds up: if you're paying, it's like rent; if you're being paid, it's a small income. It also shows the crowd's mood. Very high funding means almost everyone expects a rise. Sometimes a drop followed, but there are no guarantees.
cards.example: In real life: a thermometer. A high temperature doesn't cure or harm anything by itself, but it tells you something has overheated.

remember: Funding is a payment between longs and shorts every few hours.
When almost everyone is long, longs usually pay.
It's small for a quick trade, but it adds up on a long one.

quiz.q: Almost all traders have opened longs. Who most likely pays funding?
options: Shorts pay longs
Longs pay shorts
The exchange pays everyone
No one pays
quiz.why: When a spot in the “line for a rise” is popular, it gets more expensive. Longs pay shorts extra.

quiz.q: A $1,000 trade with 0.01% funding. How much is that per payment?
options: 10 cents
quiz.why: 1% of $1,000 is $10, and 0.01% is 100 times less: 10 cents.

quiz.q: Why does funding exist at all?
options: It's the app's income
It's a penalty for losing trades
It pulls the futures price toward the price of the coin itself
It's a government tax
quiz.why: Funding is like a rubber band: if the futures price drifts away from the coin's price, the payment pulls it back. Traders pay each other.

lessons.title: How to read a CRYPTO NOVA trade: a real example
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to read a system trade and understand what every number means.

cards.title: A real example: ARB
cards.text: Let's break down a real system trade on the demo account. Coin: ARB. Direction: up (LONG). Entry: $0.1755. Stop: $0.1544. Target: $0.2632. The trade was opened on the evening of October 18, 2026. There was one more rule: if neither the stop nor the target was hit within 24 hours, exit on time.
cards.example: In real life: you put a pie in the oven and decide: I'll take it out in 40 minutes, even if it isn't golden yet. A time exit is that kind of timer.

chart.caption: ARB trade: stop, entry and target, price in dollars

cards.title: Why the system went in
cards.text: The reason was a sharp sell-off. The price quickly fell 1.5%, while trading was almost 3 times higher than usual. In the past, dips like this were often bought back within a day. Often — but not always. In the app, this is explained in the “Why we entered” block.
cards.example: In real life: late in the day at the market, a seller in a hurry lets a crate of strawberries go cheap. Buyers snap them all up quickly, and the price goes back to normal.

cards.title: Risk and target in percent
cards.text: From entry to stop: $0.1755 − $0.1544 = $0.0211. That's about 12%. From entry to target: $0.2632 − $0.1755 = $0.0877, about 50%. The target is about 4 times further away than the stop. In the app, these numbers are in the “Risk” block: “to stop,” “to target,” “reward / risk.”
cards.example: In real life: you're willing to risk $12 for a shot at getting $50. That's a smarter bet than the other way around.

cards.title: How it ended
cards.text: Within 24 hours, neither the stop nor the target was hit. On the evening of October 19, 2026, the trade was closed on time at around $0.192 — 9.6% above the entry. This is one example, not a promise: the next trade could close at the stop.
cards.example: Let's do the math: about $2,000 of the $10,000 went into the trade. $2,000 × 9.6% ≈ $192 — that's about 1.9% of the whole demo account.

cards.title: If the entry has already passed
cards.text: Say you saw the trade late, when the price was already $0.1937. The stop is still at $0.1544 — now about 20% away, not 12%. The target is about 36% away, not 50%. The risk has grown, and the room to gain has shrunk. It's calmer to skip it and wait for the next trade.
cards.example: In real life: the bus has left. Running after it down the road is dangerous. It's calmer to wait for the next one.

cards.title: A loss is normal
cards.text: Not every trade ends in profit. Some close at the stop, and that's part of the plan. The system can be wrong, and past results don't promise future ones. That's why “Closed” shows every trade, winners and losers alike. Real money is for 18+ only.
cards.example: In real life: even a good soccer player misses the goal sometimes. What counts is the score over the season, not one shot.

remember: A trade has a coin, a direction, an entry, a stop, a target and a reason.
If the price has moved far from the entry, don't chase it — wait for the next trade.
A trade closed at the stop is part of the plan, not a failure.

quiz.q: What does the stop show in a trade?
options: The price where you take profit
The price where the trade closes with a small loss
The best price to enter at
The time when the trade ends
quiz.why: The stop is an exit decided in advance, in case the idea doesn't work out. For ARB, it's $0.1544, about 12% below the entry.

quiz.q: The trade's entry is $0.1755, but the price is already $0.1937. What's the smarter move?
options: Get in fast before the price climbs even higher
Get in and remove the stop
Go all in, since the trade is a winner
Skip it: the risk has grown, and the room to the target has shrunk
quiz.why: The stop is now about 20% away instead of 12%, and the target about 36% instead of 50%. More risk, less room. Better to wait for a new trade.

quiz.q: A trade closed at the stop. How should you see it?
options: It's a normal part of trading: the loss was limited in advance
Trades don't work; give it all up
Immediately open a trade twice as big to win it back
Move the stop further away next time
quiz.why: Everyone has losses. The stop limited the loss in advance. Trying to win it back with a big trade is the road to big losses.

lessons.title: Risk and reward: the R ratio
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will be able to judge a trade before entering: how much you can lose and how much you can gain.

cards.title: Two numbers before entering
cards.text: Before a trade, work out how much you lose if the stop is hit and how much you gain if the price reaches the target. The ratio of reward to risk is called R. Risk $50, target $100 — that is 1:2.
cards.example: In real life: before a trip you weigh what the road costs against what the trip gives.

cards.title: You can be wrong more often
cards.text: At 1:2 one winning trade covers two losing ones. 10 trades: 4 win $100 each and 6 lose $50 each. Result: $400 − $300 = +$100.
cards.example: In real life: a seller whom not everyone buys from, but every sale pays.

chart.caption: 10 trades at 1:2: 4 winners, 6 losers, $

cards.title: The target must be realistic
cards.text: A pretty 1:5 on paper is useless if the price almost never gets there. The target goes at the nearest strong zone, not where you would like it to be.
cards.example: In real life: a plan to «lose 20 kg in a week» looks great but does not work.

cards.title: Fees count too
cards.text: Fees and slippage eat part of R. On very short trades with a small target they can eat the whole profit.
cards.example: In real life: driving to another city for a cheap item — and the whole saving goes on petrol.

remember: R is the ratio of possible reward to risk.
At 1:2 you can be wrong more often than right and still be up.
A realistic target, fees included.

quiz.q: Stop −$40, target +$120. What is the ratio?
quiz.why: $120 ÷ $40 = 3. Each dollar of risk stands against three dollars of possible gain: 1:3.

quiz.q: 10 trades at 1:2 with $50 risk. 4 win, 6 lose. Result?
What is wrong with a 1:5 target the price almost never reaches?
options: Nothing
It looks good on paper but almost never works
It is too close
The exchange forbids it
quiz.why: A ratio only means something if the target is reachable. Otherwise trades close at the stop more often.

lessons.title: Order types: market, limit, stop
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will know which order to pick in which situation.

cards.title: Market order
cards.text: Buys or sells right away at the best available price. Fast, but the price may turn out slightly worse than expected — this is called slippage.
cards.example: In real life: you take an item off the shelf at the price on the tag right now.

cards.title: Limit order
cards.text: You set the price: «buy bitcoin at no more than $80,000». The order waits for the price to get there and may never fill. Its fee is often lower.
cards.example: In real life: you ask the seller to tell you when the item drops to your price.

cards.title: Stop order
cards.text: It triggers when the price reaches a set level and closes the position. That is how a stop-loss is set in advance, without sitting at the screen. In a sharp move the fill can be worse than the level.
cards.example: In real life: you buckle the seat belt before the trip, not during the crash.

cards.title: Which to choose
cards.text: Not in a hurry — limit. Need to get out right now — market. Protection from a big loss — a stop placed right when you enter the trade.
cards.example: In real life: you haggle at the market when you have time, and pay at once when the train leaves in five minutes.

remember: Market — at once, but with slippage.
Limit — at your price, but may not fill.
The stop is set right at entry.

quiz.q: You want to buy only at $80,000 or cheaper. Which order?
options: Market
Limit
Stop
None
quiz.why: A limit order fills only at your price or better.

quiz.q: What is slippage?
options: A withdrawal fee
A fill at a worse price than expected
Cancelling an order
An exchange bonus
quiz.why: In a fast market or with little volume the order «slips» to the next available price.

quiz.q: When should you set a stop-loss?
options: Right when entering the trade
When the loss gets big
Never
A week later
quiz.why: The maximum loss is decided with a cool head — before the price has gone against you.

lessons.title: Support and resistance levels
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will understand the zones on the chart and how the stop and target are placed from them.

cards.title: Where the price turned
cards.text: Support is a level below the price where buyers used to stop it from falling. Resistance is a level above where sellers used to stop it from rising. These are zones, not exact lines.
cards.example: In real life: the floor and ceiling of a room — a ball bounces off them until it breaks through.

cards.title: Why they work
cards.text: Many people remember these prices and place orders there. The more often the price turned at a level, the more visible it is. But any level can break.
cards.example: In real life: a queue forms at the same checkout where people saw one yesterday.

cards.title: Breakouts and role reversal
cards.text: If the price confidently breaks resistance, it often becomes support — and the other way round. A breakout is confirmed by a candle closing beyond the level, not by one short spike.
cards.example: In real life: the ceiling of the ground floor is the floor of the first floor.

cards.title: How CRYPTO NOVA uses them
cards.text: In the app the zones are drawn on the chart. The stop goes beyond a zone, the target at the next zone. That way the risk is known before entering the trade.
cards.example: In real life: a route is planned by landmarks, not at random.

remember: Support is below the price, resistance above.
A level is a zone, and any level can break.
Broken resistance often becomes support.

quiz.q: Where is support usually found?
options: Above the current price
Below the current price
It is trading volume
It is news
quiz.why: Support is a zone below the price where buyers used to show up.

quiz.q: The price broke resistance confidently and closed above it. What does that level often become?
options: Support
Nothing
The exchange's stop
A target
quiz.why: Former resistance often turns into support: buyers show up there again.

quiz.q: Where is it sensible to put the stop when buying at support?
options: Just below the support zone
In the middle of the zone
Above the entry price
Nowhere
quiz.why: A stop beyond the zone triggers only if the support really broke.

levels.level_sub: How to judge a system — and yourself — the way professionals do

lessons.title: How to judge a system: win rate and the average trade
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to tell whether a system is any good from two simple numbers.

cards.title: A pretty number that misleads
cards.text: Say someone tells you: “The system wins 9 trades out of 10.” Sounds great. This is called the win rate, and here it's 90%. But this number alone isn't enough. It doesn't tell you how much was won and how much was lost.
cards.example: In real life: a team spends 90% of the match in front of the other team's goal, but loses 0–3. The score is what counts, not the time spent near the goal.

cards.title: 9 small wins and 1 big disaster
cards.text: Example: 9 trades made +$10 each. That's 9 × $10 = $90 in total. One trade closed at −$200. Add it up: $90 − $200 = −$110. A 90% win rate, and the account is in the red. One big loss ate everything and then some.
cards.example: In real life: 9 days in a row, you find $10. On the 10th day, you lose a wallet with $200 in it. Lots of happy days, but you have less money.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: a $1,000 account after 10 trades

cards.title: The average trade is the key number
cards.text: Add up the results of all the trades and divide by how many there were. That gives you the average result of one trade. Pros call it “expected value.” In our example, −$110 ÷ 10 = −$11: each trade lost $11 on average. If the average is above zero, the system made money in the past.
cards.example: In real life: for a shop, the average sale matters. 100 sales of $1 bring in $100, but 10 sales of $20 bring in $200.

cards.title: You can lose more often and still be up
cards.text: Another example, again 10 trades. 4 wins of +$60: 4 × $60 = $240. 6 losses of −$20: 6 × $20 = $120. Total: $240 − $120 = +$120. Only a 40% win rate, but the average trade is +$12. The secret is simple: small losses, big wins.
cards.example: In real life: a salesperson hears “no” a lot. But one big sale makes up for 6 small rejections.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: 4 wins out of 10, and still in profit

cards.title: Few trades, little truth
cards.text: Flip a coin 10 times, and it lands heads 7 times. That doesn't mean the coin is special. It's the same with a system: 10 trades is too few. Look at hundreds of trades. In CRYPTO NOVA, a trade's “Rule history” block shows how many trades there were, how many were in profit, and the average result.
cards.example: In real life: you don't judge a café by one lunch. You need to go back many times.

remember: A win rate means nothing without the size of the wins and losses.
Average trade = the sum of all results ÷ the number of trades.
Judge a system by hundreds of trades, not by ten.

quiz.q: A system won 9 trades out of 10. What does that tell you?
options: The system is definitely profitable
The next trade will win too
Nothing yet: you need to know the size of the wins and losses
You can invest all your savings
quiz.why: One big loss can eat up 9 small wins. The win rate tells you how often, but not how much.

quiz.q: 5 trades made +$50 in total. What's the average trade?
quiz.why: Divide the total result by the number of trades: $50 ÷ 5 = $10.

quiz.q: A system wins 40% of its trades. Can it still be in profit?
options: Yes, if the winning trades are much bigger than the losing ones
No, because it wins less than half the time
No, you need at least a 60% win rate
Only if the whole market is rising
quiz.why: Example: 4 wins of $60 and 6 losses of $20 add up to +$120. Size matters, not just how often.

lessons.title: The math of drawdowns
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why pros protect their money first and think about profit second.

cards.title: What a drawdown is
cards.text: A drawdown is how far an account has fallen from its highest point. Example: it was $1,000, and now it's $800. Losing $200 of $1,000 is −20%. The “Futures” tab has a “Drawdown” tile — it's the first number pros look at.
cards.example: In real life: you climbed to the 10th floor, then went back down to the 8th. You're still high up, but you'll have to climb those 2 floors again.

cards.title: Minus and plus aren't the same
cards.text: Example: you have $100. The price falls 50%, leaving $50. Then it rises 50%. But 50% of $50 is only $25. So you end up with $50 + $25 = $75, not $100. To get back to $100, you need to double the $50. That's +100%.
cards.example: In real life: a $100 jacket at a 50%-off sale costs $50. Raise the price by 50%, and it's $75, not $100.

cards.title: A table worth remembering
cards.text: −10% → you need +11.1% to get back. −25% → you need +33.3%. −50% → you need +100%. −90% → you need +900%. The deeper the hole, the steeper the climb. After −90%, $1,000 becomes $100. To get back to $1,000, it has to grow 10 times over.
cards.example: In real life: you can step out of a hole 1 meter deep. But you can't get out of a 10-meter hole without a long ladder.

chart.caption: How much growth (%) you need to get back after a drop

cards.title: Why it works this way
cards.text: Growth is counted from what's left, not from what you had. After losses, you have less money. So each percent of growth brings in fewer dollars. That's why falling is easy and climbing back takes a long time.
cards.example: In real life: you can run down a mountain in 10 minutes. Climbing back up the same mountain takes an hour.

cards.title: The pros' main rule: protection first
cards.text: Example: you risk 1% of your account per trade. 10 losses in a row come to about −10%, which is easy enough to recover from. Risk 10% per trade, and after 10 losses, about 35% of the account is left. To get back, you'd need almost +190%. That's why every trade gets a stop and risks only a small slice of the account.
cards.example: In real life: a seatbelt doesn't make the trip faster. But it saves you on the one day there's a crash.

remember: −50% takes +100% to recover, and −90% takes +900%.
Growth is counted from what's left, so climbing back is always harder than falling.
A small risk on every trade is the best protection for your account.

quiz.q: An account fell 50%. How much does it need to grow to get back?
quiz.why: It was $100, now it's $50. For $50 to become $100 again, it has to double. That's +100%.

quiz.q: What is a drawdown?
options: The total of all losing trades over a year
An account's fall from its highest point
An exchange fee for a trade
Bitcoin's price drop in a single day
quiz.why: A drawdown shows how far an account has dropped from its peak. The deeper it is, the harder it is to get back.

quiz.q: Why do pros risk only a small part of their account on one trade?
options: So they pay the exchange less
Small trades win more often
So a losing streak doesn't dig a deep hole
Because the law requires it
quiz.why: With 1% risk, even 10 losses in a row come to about −10%. A hole like that is much easier to climb out of.

lessons.title: Testing on history and the overfitting trap
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll be able to tell an honest test of a system from a pretty overfit one.

cards.title: Testing on history
cards.text: Before trading by a rule, you test it on past prices. You take years of history and see what would have happened if the rule had been in use back then. This is called a backtest. CRYPTO NOVA tests new versions of its rules this way every night.
cards.example: In real life: before cooking dinner for guests, you think back to how the dish turned out before.

cards.title: The overfitting trap
cards.text: You can keep tweaking a rule until it shows a perfect result on history. For example: “buy on Tuesdays at 2:05 p.m. if it rained the day before.” It worked in the past, but that's just coincidence. This mistake is called overfitting. In the future, it almost always lets you down.
cards.example: In real life: a key filed down to fit one lock exactly. It opens only that lock. It won't fit any other door.

cards.title: An exam with new questions
cards.text: How do you test honestly? You split the history into 2 parts. On the first, you come up with the rule. On the second, you test it. The rule hasn't “seen” this data yet. If the result is good there too, you can trust the rule more. But there are still no guarantees.
cards.example: In real life: a student memorized the answers to last year's test and scored 100%. Give them new questions, and you'll see right away whether they understand the subject.

cards.title: Signs of overfitting
cards.text: Be wary if there are almost no losses in the history. Or if the account's line is perfectly smooth. Or if there are very few trades. Or if the rule has dozens of conditions. Real trading always comes with losses. A result that's too pretty usually points to overfitting, not genius.
cards.example: In real life: if a café has nothing but 5-star reviews, it's too good to be true. Honest reviews are always mixed.

cards.title: Why we show losses too
cards.text: The market changes like the weather. What worked yesterday may stop working tomorrow. That's why it's important to see the whole truth. In CRYPTO NOVA, you can see every closed trade, including the losing ones, and the account's drawdown. And “Rule history” separately shows how the rule has done live.
cards.example: In real life: an honest doctor tells you not only about a medicine's benefits, but also about its side effects.

remember: A backtest checks a rule against past prices.
Overfitting is a rule that knows the past by heart but doesn't understand the market.
An honest test uses data the rule hasn't seen.

quiz.q: What is a backtest?
options: A trade with a small amount
Testing a rule on past prices
A price forecast for tomorrow
A test of the app's speed
quiz.why: A backtest shows what would have happened if the rule had been in use before. Like checking a recipe against past dinners.

quiz.q: On history, a rule won 100% of its trades with not a single loss. What does that most likely mean?
options: The perfect system has been found
The market won't fall anymore
It's time to invest all your savings
The rule has been overfitted to the past
