quiz.why: Real trading always comes with losses. A perfect result on history usually points to overfitting.

quiz.q: What's a more honest way to test a rule?
options: On a part of history the rule hasn't seen
Again, on the same data
By adding more conditions
By asking friends what they think
quiz.why: New data is like an exam with new questions. It shows whether the rule actually works, or just memorized the past.

lessons.title: Macro: interest rates, the dollar and crypto
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand why news about US interest rates and prices moves crypto.

cards.title: What macro is
cards.text: Macro is the big picture of the economy. How much loans cost. How fast prices in stores are rising. Whether the dollar is strong. This affects every market at once: stocks, gold and crypto.
cards.example: In real life: the weather affects the whole city. In a downpour, parks, sidewalk cafés and markets all empty out.

cards.title: The interest rate is the price of money
cards.text: A country's central bank sets the main interest rate. It decides what interest banks charge on loans. The rate is the price of money. A high rate means money is expensive. A low rate means it's cheap. The US central bank is called the Federal Reserve, or the Fed. As of October 2026: in September 2026 the Fed raised its rate to 3.75–4% a year, its first hike since 2023.
cards.example: Example: a $10,000 loan at 5% a year costs $500 in interest. At 20%, it's $2,000. When loans are expensive, people take them out less often.

cards.title: Cheap money and risk
cards.text: When money is cheap, a bank deposit earns very little. People look for ways to earn more and buy riskier things more often: stocks, crypto. When money is expensive, deposits pay off again, and many people move away from risk. This has often been the case, but not always.
cards.example: In real life: if a deposit pays 1% a year, many people start thinking about property or stocks. If it pays 10%, it's easier to just keep the money in the bank.

cards.title: Inflation and the dollar
cards.text: Inflation is rising prices in stores. If it's high, the Fed may keep rates high. That's why the whole market waits for US inflation reports. And when the dollar gets stronger against other currencies, crypto often weakens. But not always.
cards.example: Example: a year ago, a basket of groceries cost $100; now it's $110. That's 10% inflation. The same money buys less.

cards.title: News days: be careful
cards.text: On days of Fed decisions and inflation reports, the price can jump sharply either way, sometimes within minutes. The dates of this news are known in advance. Pros are careful during these hours: they trade smaller or wait. No one knows which way the market will go.
cards.example: In real life: a fisherman doesn't head out to sea when a storm warning has been issued. Even if the storm might pass by.

remember: The interest rate is the price of money. Cheap money tends to push people toward risk.
Fed and inflation news can swing the price sharply either way.
Macro explains the background, but it doesn't tell you exactly where the price will go.

quiz.q: What is a central bank's interest rate, in plain words?
options: Bitcoin's exchange rate against the dollar
A tax on purchases
The price of money: it sets the interest on loans
An exchange fee for a trade
quiz.why: The main rate determines the interest on loans and deposits. A high rate means money is expensive; a low rate means it's cheap.

quiz.q: Money has become cheap, and deposits pay very little. How do people often behave?
options: They buy riskier things more often, like stocks and crypto
Everyone sells their stocks at once
They stop spending money
Nothing changes
quiz.why: When deposits pay little, people look for ways to earn more. This has often been the case, but not always.

quiz.q: There's a Fed decision this evening. What's sensible to keep in mind?
options: The price will definitely rise, so you can put everything in
News doesn't affect crypto
Better to take out a loan and buy crypto in advance
The price may jump sharply either way, so be careful
quiz.why: On big news days, the price often jumps around. No one knows the direction in advance, so pros reduce their risk.

lessons.title: On-chain: tracking the whales
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand what you can see on the blockchain and why conclusions should be drawn carefully.

cards.title: An open notebook
cards.text: A blockchain is a shared notebook of transfers. Anyone can read it. You can see how many coins were sent and where. There are no names, only addresses — long strings of letters and numbers. Studying these records is called on-chain analysis: looking at what's recorded “on the chain.”
cards.example: In real life: see-through mailboxes with numbers on them. You can see how many letters came in. But you can't see who owns the mailbox.

cards.title: Who the whales are
cards.text: A whale is someone who holds a huge number of coins. It could be a wealthy person, a fund or an exchange itself. When a whale moves coins, everyone can see the transfer. Many traders keep an eye on transfers like these.
cards.example: In real life: a wholesale buyer comes to the market and buys up all the potatoes. Every seller notices right away.

cards.title: A whale moved coins to an exchange
cards.text: Example: a whale sent 1,000 bitcoins to an exchange. At a price of $80,000, that's 1,000 × $80,000 = $80,000,000. Many people think: he wants to sell. That does happen, since selling usually happens on an exchange. If he sells a lot, the price may drop. But that's just one explanation.
cards.example: In real life: a farmer brings a whole truckload of apples to the market. Most likely, he's going to sell. And apples may get cheaper that day.

cards.title: Why it's not always so
cards.text: Transfers to an exchange happen for other reasons too. An exchange moves its own coins around. A whale puts coins up as collateral for a loan. A fund switches to a different storage provider. And sometimes a whale moves coins and then changes his mind. A transfer is a clue, not a verdict.
cards.example: In real life: your neighbor carries suitcases out of the house. Maybe he's moving. Or maybe he's going on vacation, or taking things to his summer house.

cards.title: How to look at on-chain data sensibly
cards.text: One transfer proves nothing. Look at several signs together: the price, trading volume, the news. The opposite happens too: coins leave exchanges for personal wallets. That's often seen as a sign that people plan to hold them for a long time. But there are no guarantees here either.
cards.example: In real life: a doctor doesn't make a diagnosis from a temperature alone. They look at test results, symptoms and medical history.

remember: The blockchain is open: big transfers are visible to all, but there are no names.
A whale moved coins to an exchange — he may be selling, but not necessarily.
On-chain data is a hint, not a verdict. Look at several signs together.

quiz.q: What can you see on the blockchain?
options: The owner's name and passport
How many coins were sent, and to which address
Where the price will go tomorrow
Wallet passwords
quiz.why: The blockchain shows transfers between addresses. There are no names there, and no forecasts either.

quiz.q: A whale moved a lot of bitcoin to an exchange. What's an honest conclusion?
options: He'll definitely sell, and the price will fall
The price will definitely rise
He may be selling, but there could be other reasons
Transfers like this never affect anything
quiz.why: A transfer to an exchange is often linked to selling. But exchanges move their own coins around, and funds switch storage.

quiz.q: Who is called a “whale”?
options: Someone who holds a huge number of coins
A beginner with a small account
A program that looks for trades
Any exchange employee
quiz.why: A whale is a big holder: a person, a fund or an exchange. Their transfers stand out because the amounts are large.

lessons.title: Psychology: fear, greed and FOMO
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll recognize your own emotions in the market and know how to keep them from deciding for you.

cards.title: The market's two main emotions
cards.text: People move the market. And people are often moved by 2 feelings: fear and greed. Fear whispers: “Sell, it'll get worse.” Greed whispers: “Buy, everyone else has already made money.” Both voices are loudest at the worst possible moment.
cards.example: In real life: at a sale, we're happy about low prices. But in the market, when everything gets cheaper, many people sell in a panic.

cards.title: The Fear and Greed Index
cards.text: There's an index that measures the market's mood as a number from 0 to 100. Near 0 means extreme fear. Near 100 means extreme greed. In the middle is calm. On Home, you'll find it in the “Sentiment” tile.
cards.example: In real life: it's like a thermometer. It doesn't cure anything or predict anything, but it shows whether there's a fever.

cards.title: The cycle of emotions
cards.text: The price rises — people get excited and buy more. Right at the peak, greed is at its strongest. Then the price falls, and excitement turns into fear. At the very bottom, many sell in a panic. And then the market often turns around — without them.
cards.example: In real life: on a roller coaster, people scream with delight at the top and with fear at the bottom. Meanwhile, the car just keeps rolling along its tracks.

chart.caption: Illustrative example: market mood by month, from 0 to 100

cards.title: FOMO: the fear of missing out
cards.text: FOMO is the fear of missing out on a profit. Your friends are bragging: a coin has tripled. You want in before it's too late. You buy after the rise has already happened, often near the top. Buying out of FOMO means buying out of greed, not by plan.
cards.example: Example: Anna bought a coin at $3 after it rose from $1. A month later, the price is $2. She's scared, so she sells. That's −$1 on every coin. And then the price starts rising again.

cards.title: Rules set in advance
cards.text: Pros decide everything before a trade, with a calm head: where the entry is, where the stop is, where the target is, and how much money goes in. When the market gets noisy, they just follow the plan. The emotions don't go away. But the plan makes the decisions, not the mood. The Piggy bank works the same way, by the way: buying on a schedule, without emotion.
cards.example: In real life: you write your shopping list at home. Go to the store hungry and without a list, and you'll come home with lots of things you didn't need.

remember: Fear pushes you to sell at the bottom; greed and FOMO push you to buy at the top.
The Fear and Greed Index is a mood thermometer, not a forecast.
Write your rules in advance, and during a trade, simply follow them.

quiz.q: The Fear and Greed Index shows 95. What does that mean?
options: The price will definitely keep rising
There's extreme fear in the market
It's time to invest all your savings
There's extreme greed in the market, and many people are buying on emotion
quiz.why: Near 100 means extreme greed. It's a mood thermometer, not a promise. On days like these, it's especially easy to buy at the peak.

quiz.q: What is FOMO?
options: A way to protect your account from losses
The fear of missing out, which makes people buy after a big rise
The name of an exchange
A fee for transferring coins
quiz.why: FOMO is the fear of missing out. It pushes you to buy after the rise has already happened, often near the top.

quiz.q: How do pros deal with emotions?
options: They write rules in advance and follow them
They decide based on how they feel in the moment
They don't feel any emotions at all
They only trade when the market is rising
quiz.why: Everyone has emotions. Pros decide the entry, stop and amount in advance, and in the moment, they simply follow the plan.

lessons.title: Your trading plan on one page
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll have your own one-page plan and a checklist to run through before every trade.

cards.title: Why you need a plan
cards.text: Trading without a plan is like a road trip without a map. You'll end up somewhere, but probably not where you wanted to go. A plan fits on one page. It has 5 points: your goal, your amount, your risk per trade, when to stop, and a journal. Write it while the market is calm.
cards.example: In real life: before renovating, you make a budget. Otherwise, the money runs out halfway, and the walls are left without wallpaper.

cards.title: Goal and amount
cards.text: Your goal should be honest and calm. For example: “For 3 months, I'll learn on demo and keep a journal and a Piggy bank.” Not “double my money in a month”: a goal like that pushes you toward big risks. The amount should be only money you don't need to live on. No loans. Real money is for 18+ only.
cards.example: Example: you've set aside $500. It's not your rent or grocery money. Losing it would hurt, but it wouldn't put your family at risk.

cards.title: Risk per trade
cards.text: Decide in advance how much you can lose on one trade. Many pros risk 1–2% of their account. Example: a $500 account with 1% risk. That means $500 × 1% = $5 per trade. If the price hits your stop, you lose about $5, not half your account.
cards.example: In real life: you don't take all your money to the market, just enough for your shopping. Even if you lose your wallet, it's not a big disaster.

cards.title: When to stop
cards.text: Write down a pause rule. Example: 3 losses in a row — take a break until tomorrow. The account is down 10% for the month — stop and go over the mistakes. That way, you won't start trying to “win it back.” Anger after losses is your account's worst enemy.
cards.example: In real life: an experienced driver pulls over when tired. Better to lose half an hour than to end up in a crash.

cards.title: Trading journal
cards.text: After every trade, write down: the date, the coin, why you went in, the result and how you felt. Reread it once a week. You'll see your mistakes and your strengths. Without a journal, the same mistakes happen again and again.
cards.example: In real life: an athlete keeps a training log. After a month, you can see what helps and what just gets in the way.

cards.title: Checklist before a trade
cards.text: Before every trade, answer 5 questions. 1) Do I know why I'm going in? 2) Is my stop set? 3) Is the risk within my limit? 4) Am I calm and not in a rush? 5) Will I write this trade in my journal? Even one “no” — skip the trade.
cards.example: In real life: before takeoff, a pilot runs through a checklist, even after flying 1,000 times. It's boring, but it saves lives.

remember: Your plan: goal, amount, risk per trade, a pause rule and a journal.
Risk only a small slice of your account on one trade, for example 1–2%.
Even one “no” on the checklist — skip the trade.

quiz.q: A $1,000 account with 2% risk per trade. How much can you lose on one trade?
quiz.why: $1,000 × 2% = $20. If the price hits your stop, you'll lose about $20, not a big chunk of your account.

quiz.q: Which goal makes more sense for a plan?
options: Double my money in a month
Spend 3 months learning on demo and keep a journal
Never miss a single rise
Make money on one coin
quiz.why: A calm goal doesn't push you toward big risks. Chasing a quick double often leads to big losses.

quiz.q: You've had 3 losses in a row and want to win it back right away. What does a good plan say?
options: Increase the amount to get it all back faster
Remove the stop so there are no more losses
Take a break and go over the trades in your journal
Buy the coin everyone is talking about
quiz.why: Wanting to win it back is an emotion. The pause rule protects your account, and the journal helps you find the mistake.

lessons.title: Expectancy: why 40% winners can be profitable
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will be able to work out whether a system earns on average per trade.

cards.title: The formula in one line
cards.text: Expectancy is the average result of one trade over the long run: win rate × average gain − loss rate × average loss.
cards.example: In real life: a fisherman's average catch over many trips, not one lucky Saturday.

cards.title: An example
cards.example: In real life: a shop can sell less often but at a better price — and earn more than its neighbour.

chart.caption: Average result of one trade, $

cards.title: You need many trades
cards.text: Expectancy shows over dozens and hundreds of trades. Over five, chance decides. That is why a system is judged on a large sample, fees included.
cards.example: In real life: one coin toss does not tell you whether the coin is fair.

cards.title: The win-rate trap
cards.text: A high win rate means nothing on its own. If the rare loss is huge, it eats all the small gains. Look at expectancy and the worst drawdown together.
cards.example: In real life: picking up coins in front of a steamroller — frequent and pleasant, until it rolls over you.

remember: Expectancy = win rate × average gain − loss rate × average loss.
You can win less often and still earn.
Judge on a large sample, fees included.

quiz.q: 50% winners at +$100, 50% losers at −$60. Expectancy?
A system wins 80% of trades. What else do you need to know to judge it?
options: Nothing, it is profitable
The average gain and the average loss
The colour of the chart
The number of followers
quiz.why: Without the size of gains and losses the win rate does not tell you whether the system earns.

quiz.q: Why are 5 trades too few to judge?
options: Over a short stretch chance decides
The exchange does not count them
It is too many
There are no fees
quiz.why: Chance easily gives 5 wins in a row. You need dozens and hundreds of trades.

lessons.title: Correlation: when diversification fails
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will see why 10 altcoins are not 10 different risks.

cards.title: Moving together
cards.text: Correlation shows how much assets move together: from −1 (opposite) to +1 (the same way). Most altcoins are strongly tied to bitcoin.
cards.example: In real life: umbrellas and raincoats sell on the same days.

cards.title: The illusion of variety
cards.text: 10 different altcoins are not 10 different risks. When bitcoin falls, nearly everything usually falls. A portfolio of similar coins behaves like one big coin.
cards.example: In real life: ten eggs in different baskets, but all the baskets in one car.

cards.title: Ties tighten in a panic
cards.text: On normal days coins move differently, but in a sharp fall correlation rises: everything is sold at once. That is exactly when protection is needed.
cards.example: In real life: in a fire everyone runs for all the doors at once, not in turn.

cards.title: What really spreads the risk
cards.text: Things of a different nature: dollars, yield-bearing stablecoins, gold, market-neutral strategies. Their returns are lower, but they do not fall together with crypto. There are no guarantees here either.
cards.example: In real life: an umbrella and sunscreen — something will come in handy in any weather.

remember: Correlation is how much assets move together.
Altcoins are usually strongly tied to bitcoin.
In a panic ties tighten — you need a different type of asset.

quiz.q: A correlation of +1 means the assets…
options: Move the same way
Move in opposite ways
Are not related at all
Are both stablecoins
quiz.why: +1 is a full match in direction, −1 is the full opposite.

quiz.q: Bitcoin is falling. A portfolio of 10 altcoins usually…
options: Rises
Falls too
Does not change
Doubles
quiz.why: Altcoins are strongly tied to bitcoin and usually lose even more in falls.

quiz.q: What spreads the risk of a crypto portfolio better?
options: 10 more altcoins
Dollars and market-neutral strategies
Meme coins
Leverage
quiz.why: Risk is spread by assets of a different nature that do not fall together with crypto.

lessons.title: Volatility and position size
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will be able to size a trade so that the risk in dollars stays the same.

cards.title: What volatility is
cards.text: Volatility is how strongly the price swings. Bitcoin's usual daily move is 2–4%; small altcoins can move 10% or more.
cards.example: In real life: a calm river and a mountain stream — you can swim in both, but differently.

cards.title: Same risk — different size
cards.text: If the stop is set by volatility, a wild coin gets a wider stop. To risk the same $50, the position in the wild coin is smaller: a 2% stop — a $2,500 position, a 10% stop — $500.
cards.example: In real life: on ice you take small steps, on asphalt normal ones.

chart.caption: Position size for a $50 risk, $

cards.title: Volatility changes
cards.text: Calm weeks give way to stormy ones. A sensible system cuts the size when the market is stormy and does not raise it just because the last trades went well.
cards.example: In real life: you do not go to sea in a small boat during a storm, even if yesterday was calm.

cards.title: How CRYPTO NOVA does it
cards.text: The autopilot sizes each trade to volatility and keeps the total risk within the risk shield's limits. That does not cancel losses, but one wild coin does not decide the fate of the whole account.
cards.example: In real life: the load is spread across the whole boat, not put on one side.

remember: Volatility is the strength of price swings.
For the same risk in $, the position in a wild coin is smaller.
In a storm the size is cut.

quiz.q: Risk $30, stop 3%. What position size?
quiz.why: $30 ÷ 3% = $1,000. If the stop is hit, the loss is $1,000 × 3% = $30.

quiz.q: A coin became twice as wild and the stop moved twice as far. What should happen to the size to keep the risk the same?
options: Double it
Cut it roughly in half
Leave it
Remove the stop
quiz.why: A stop twice as far means a size half as big — and the loss in dollars stays the same.

quiz.q: Bitcoin's usual daily move is roughly…
quiz.why: In calm periods bitcoin usually moves 2–4% a day. Small coins move more.

lessons.title: Yield on dollars: where the interest comes from and where the risk is
lessons.goal: By the end, you'll understand where stablecoin yield comes from and why it never comes without risk.

cards.title: Where the interest comes from
cards.text: Stablecoins can do more than sit there: you can lend them through blockchain services such as Aave. The interest is paid by borrowers — most often traders who need dollars against their coins as collateral. When many people want to borrow, the rate goes up. When few do, it drops to a couple of percent.
cards.example: Example: $1,000 at 5% a year earns about $50 a year. But the rate floats: a month later it could be 3% or 8%.

cards.title: Other sources
cards.text: There are also savings stablecoins, where the service itself pays the rate out of its income, for example Sky. And Ethena's “yield-bearing dollar” sUSDe earns mostly from funding — payments between futures traders. While traders pay a lot, the yield is high. When the market falls, it can drop almost to zero.
cards.example: In real life: a bank pays interest on deposits while it earns on loans itself. When borrowers struggle, the interest falls too.

cards.title: Where the risk is
cards.text: A bug in the code — and hackers can drain the money. A stablecoin can lose its $1 peg. The service or the issuer can freeze coins. There's no insurance like on a bank deposit. The higher the promised yield, the bigger the hidden risk.
cards.example: In real life: a bank offering 20% a year when everyone else pays 5% is a reason to be wary, not to celebrate.

cards.title: How CRYPTO NOVA does it
cards.text: The CRYPTO NOVA public portfolio has a “Dollar yield” source: lending USDC and USDT through Aave and Sky. As of October 2026, that's about 15% of the portfolio, plus about 5% in Ethena sUSDe. It's a demo at real rates. The shares are capped so that trouble with one service doesn't hit the whole portfolio.
cards.example: In real life: eggs go in different baskets. Even if one falls, the others are fine.

remember: Stablecoin interest is paid by borrowers or by the service itself — the rate floats.
Risks: hacks, losing the $1 peg, freezes. There's no insurance.
There's no high yield without risk.

quiz.q: Who pays the interest when you lend USDC through a service?
options: The government
Borrowers who need dollars
CRYPTO NOVA
Nobody: the interest appears by itself
quiz.why: The interest is paid by those who borrow. Fewer borrowers means a lower rate.

quiz.q: A service promises 25% a year on dollars with no risk. How should you treat it?
options: It's a warning sign: there's no high yield without risk
It's a normal rate
Put everything in before the offer ends
It's dollars, so there's no risk
quiz.why: The higher the promised yield, the bigger the hidden risk. The words “no risk” are the main sign of a scam.

quiz.q: Why shouldn't you keep all your dollars in one service?
options: The rate is higher that way
Services forbid it
If it gets hacked or frozen, all your money is hit
It's inconvenient
quiz.why: These services have no deposit insurance. Spreading across services limits the damage.

lessons.title: Options in plain words
lessons.goal: After this lesson you will know what a put and a call are, why insurance against a fall costs money every month and why CRYPTO NOVA does not trade options.

cards.title: Put and call
cards.text: An option is an insurance policy on a price. A put gives the right to sell bitcoin at a price chosen in advance, even if it has fallen below it. A call is the right to buy at the chosen price, even if it has risen above it. The right costs a premium. If the right was not needed, the premium is lost in full.
cards.example: In real life: car insurance. You pay every year. No accident — the money is not returned. An accident — the insurer pays.

cards.title: Why a put earns in a fall
cards.text: You bought a put with the right to sell BTC at 70,000 when it cost 78,000. BTC fell to 55,000. The right to sell at 70,000 is now worth about 15,000 per BTC: the gap between 70,000 and 55,000. That is how people «earn on a fall». BTC stayed above 70,000 — the put expired empty, the premium is gone.
cards.example: In real life: fire insurance on a house. The house burned — you got the payout. It did not — you simply paid every year.

cards.title: The premium is the price of insurance
cards.text: A 30-day put protecting against a fall deeper than 10% usually costs 2–5% of the BTC price. A month later the insurance must be bought again. Over a year that adds up to about 17–25% of the sum. Just to break even, the fall has to be strong and on time — while the policy is valid.
cards.example: Example: BTC 78,000, a put with the right to sell at 70,000 costs 2,000. The profit starts only below 68,000: 70,000 minus the 2,000 premium.

cards.title: Why most buyers lose
cards.text: An option gets cheaper every day — this is time decay. The insurance is renewed again and again, while strong falls are rare. On BTC history 2023–2026, only 5 of 27 puts bought expired in the money. All 3 big falls began while our indicator still showed «growth»: the put was bought only after the first −15…−25%.
cards.example: In real life: people buy an umbrella once they are already wet. By then the rain often stops.

cards.title: What history says
cards.text: Tested on BTC from 2023 to October 2026. Just holding BTC: +369%, drawdown −53%. Our rule «regime «fall» → USDT»: +218%, drawdown −18.5%. Holding and buying a put in a «fall»: +235%, the same −53% drawdown, 17% a year in premiums. The insurance did not cut the drawdown; moving to USDT did, with no premiums.
cards.example: In real life: in India millions of private traders use options. The regulator counted 89–93% losing over a year. The seller of the premium earns more often than the buyer.

cards.title: Why CRYPTO NOVA does not trade them
cards.text: 3 reasons. There are no options on OKX Europe — our real account in the EU cannot see them. OKX copy trading copies only futures and spot: subscribers would not receive options trades. And on history they improved neither the result nor the drawdown. So for us options are knowledge and a mood indicator only.
cards.example: In real life: a tool may be interesting, but if your shop does not sell it and it does not help, there is no reason to buy it.

cards.title: The indicator on the panel
cards.text: The «Options mood» tile. DVOL — how much movement in BTC the options market expects over a year; the percentile — whether that is expensive or cheap by the year's standards. Put/call — how many hedges against a fall per 1 bet on a rise. Expensive puts mean fear, often near a bottom. Cheap puts in a rise mean complacency. Information, not a signal.
cards.example: Example: DVOL 55 at the 80th percentile — the market is more frightened than on 80% of the year's days. Put/call 0.95 — almost as many hedges as bets on a rise.

remember: A put is the right to sell at a chosen price, a call the right to buy. The right costs a premium, and it is lost if the right was not needed.
A put earns in a fall, but the insurance must be bought every month: 2–5% a month, about 17–25% a year.
On 2023–2026 history puts did not reduce the drawdown (−53%), while the rule «fall → USDT» cut it to −18.5% with no premiums.
CRYPTO NOVA does not trade options: none on OKX Europe, not copied, no help on history. The panel shows a mood indicator only.

quiz.q: You bought a put with the right to sell BTC at 70,000 for a 2,000 premium. At expiry BTC is 72,000. What happens to your money?
options: You get the 2,000 back
The 2,000 premium is lost in full
You earned 2,000
You receive 70,000
quiz.why: BTC is above 70,000, so the right to sell at 70,000 was not needed. The policy expired, the premium is lost.

quiz.q: Why does buying puts every month usually end in a loss?
options: Exchanges forbid buying puts
An option gets cheaper every day, and strong falls are rare
Puts only rise in summer
The premium is always refunded
quiz.why: Time decay plus repeated payment: a 2–5% monthly premium burns, and only 5 of 27 puts expired in the money on 2023–2026 history.

options: A signal to buy or sell
The mood of the options market: DVOL and put/call, information only
CRYPTO NOVA's profit on options
The bitcoin price a month ahead
quiz.why: It is a fear-and-calm indicator. CRYPTO NOVA does not trade options; no trade follows from this tile.
